post.summary: Make somebody a service account, or a person again
post.description:
A service account is a PERSON entry carrying `stsServiceAccount` (#221): everything a person is — a password, app passwords, Kerberos keys, groups, roles, Shared Signals under their `iss_sub` — and governed by the realm's service-account policy (`GET /admin-api/policies`, kind `serviceAccount`): whether the second factor is exempt, whether a browser sign-in is allowed (not by default), which password doors open, and whether its password rotates and is pushed to a secrets manager.

`serviceAccount` true (the default) sets or changes it: `owners`, the WHOLE list of the people and groups in this realm who answer for it (#600) — it replaces the list the account names, at most 25, at least one while the policy's `requireOwner` is on; `destination`, a push destination's DN, and `secretName` go together. `serviceAccount` false makes them an ordinary person again and clears the owner, the destination and the rotation state.

Where the policy refuses a service account every browser sign-in, becoming one ENDS the person's sessions (`signedOut`). SCIM does not carry the flag; an LDAP modify by a holder of Admin Write may, under the same rules.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/users, POST /admin/users/new, POST /admin/users/edit and POST /admin/users/service-account` on the admin console.

200.description: The account as it now stands (`account`), and the sessions ended (`signedOut`).

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

serviceAccount.description: true makes or keeps them a service account (the default); false makes them a person again.

owners.description: The people and groups answerable for the account (#600), each a DN, a username or a group's cn: an array, or a string of one per line. It REPLACES the owners the account names; absent or empty is none, refused while the policy requires an owner.

destination.description: The DN of the push destination (an application entry).

secretName.description: The secret's name or path at the destination; it must already exist there.

post.summary: Export one person's entry as an LDIF file
post.description:
Answers the person's directory entry as an RFC 2849 LDIF document with one record: `ldif` (the text) and `files` (the same, named and base64, which the console saves). The attributes a create takes only — the inetOrgPerson attributes, the credential catalogue's and the realm's custom attributes, which is what `import-ldif` writes back; nothing this service recorded about the person (sign-in methods, federation sightings, consents, flags), no group membership and no `entryUUID`. The DN is the entry's own; `import-ldif` creates the person in whichever realm it is called in.

**CREDENTIAL MATERIAL IS LEFT OUT BY DEFAULT** and named in `leftOut`. With `credentials` true the password's stored hash, the authenticator app (its secret opened), the passkeys and their user handles, the recovery codes, the app passwords, the stored client certificates, the HOBA keys and the CIBA user code's hash are written **UNENCRYPTED**: a value sealed under this process's key-encryption key is opened, because a file sealed under it opens nowhere else. Keep such a file as you would the secrets in it. Kerberos keys, the RFC 7523 and RFC 7522 key pairs, enrolled certificates and enrolment secrets are never exported: each is minted by its own subsystem. An audit row (`user.export`) says whether credentials went with the file, never a value. Asked for a recent sign-in, as `set-password` is.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/users, POST /admin/users/new, POST /admin/users/edit and POST /admin/users/service-account` on the admin console.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

credentials.description: Include credential material, UNENCRYPTED. False when absent.

post.summary: Create a person from an LDIF file
post.description:
Reads an RFC 2849 LDIF document holding ONE person's record, as `export-ldif` writes it (`uid=<name>,ou=users,…` with that name as its one `uid`), and creates that person in the realm this is called in, through the create `POST /admin-api/users/create` makes: the realm's attribute policy, the username rules and one entry per person are its checks. **IT NEVER OVERWRITES**: a username already here is refused, naming the entry that holds it (STS-LDAP-0218). A new `entryUUID`, and so a new subject, is minted; a file carrying one is refused.

Only the attributes a create takes and the credentials an export writes are taken; a record carrying what this service records about a person, or a credential a subsystem mints, is refused naming each (STS-LDAP-0219). A credential in the file is written as stored: a password only as the hash this service writes (a hash cannot be held to the password policy, so a clear password is refused — set one with `set-password` after the import), the authenticator secret and a legacy recovery-code set sealed again wherever the key-encryption key persists, a passkey user handle or a stored certificate refused when somebody here holds it already (STS-LDAP-0220). **No Kerberos key is derived from a hash**: the person has none until their password is set again. A CAEP credential-change is sent for each kind of credential that came in, and the import is audited (`user.import`) with the attribute names, never a value. Give the document as `ldif` (its text), or as `file` (its name and text), which is how the console sends an uploaded file. Asked for a recent sign-in, as `set-password` is.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/users, POST /admin/users/new, POST /admin/users/edit and POST /admin/users/service-account` on the admin console.

200.description: The `username` created, its `dn`, the `attributes` the create wrote and the `credentials` written after it.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

file.description: An uploaded LDIF file: its name and its text.

version: 1

post.summary: Issue somebody a message-signing certificate from this realm's CA
post.description:
Generates a key pair and certifies it from the realm's `message-signing` Issuing CA with `digitalSignature` only and `urn:sts:person:<username>` as its subjectAltName. A WS-Trust request whose WS-Security signature over the SOAP Body and Timestamp verifies under it authenticates the person as its requester; it signs nobody in over TLS. An administrator's act: the person has no door to it on the user portal (#521).

**THIS REPLY IS THE ONLY COPY OF THE PRIVATE KEY.** `files` holds a PKCS#12 (base64), an encrypted PKCS#8 PEM key and the PEM chain, all protected by `password`, which is neither stored nor audited. Refused past `pki.messageSigningCertificateMax` valid certificates (`STS-PKI-0220`), for a person with no entry (`STS-ADMIN-0905`), for a key algorithm outside `rsa-2048`, `rsa-3072`, `ec-p256`, `ec-p384`, and in a realm with no certificate authority.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/users, POST /admin/users/new, POST /admin/users/edit and POST /admin/users/service-account` on the admin console.

200.description: The certificate (serial, subject, thumbprint, PEM and chain, its urn:sts: name), the three files, and the person's message-signing certificates as they now stand, in `signing`.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

post.summary: Enrol a self-issued (SIOPv2) subject for somebody
post.description:
Enrols a did:jwk, did:key or did:web, an RFC 9278 JWK thumbprint URI, a base64url SHA-256 JWK thumbprint or a public JWK (as JSON) on the person's entry. A self-issued ID Token signed by that key then signs them in, while oid4vp.signInSelfIssued is on. Refused where the subject is already enrolled for anybody in the realm. A person enrols their own on /portal/self-issued by proving the key with their wallet.

What this enrols is recorded as BY VALUE (`proof: admin`, unproven), and nothing that releases or binds a subject reads it. A did:web's DID document is fetched now and every authentication key it names is pinned; a later sign-in with any other key is refused (STS-VC-0126). A document that cannot be fetched or names no such key is refused (STS-ADMIN-0871) (#693).

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/users, POST /admin/users/new, POST /admin/users/edit and POST /admin/users/service-account` on the admin console.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

post.summary: Disable somebody's account, and end everything they hold
post.description:
Sets `pwdAccountLockedTime` (draft-behera-ldap-password-policy's administrative lock, `000001010000Z`) on the person's entry. From then on EVERY door refuses them, in every mode: a password anywhere (the sign-in screen, an LDAP bind, the password grant, WS-Trust, SCIM and SSF Basic, EST), a session from any sign-in (a security key, federation, SPNEGO, a TLS client certificate, the wallet), a Kerberos AS-REQ (KDC_ERR_CLIENT_REVOKED), every token grant made on their behalf (`invalid_grant`, a refresh token included), every assertion, and this API.

**Everything they hold is ended at once**, by the same global logout `POST /admin-api/logout/global` performs: sessions (with CAEP `session-revoked` and back-channel Logout Tokens to their relying parties), tokens, codes, directory connections and Kerberos tickets. RISC receivers are sent `account-disabled`. Front-channel notifications need the person's own browser and are not sent. SCIM's `active: false` is the same act.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/users, POST /admin/users/new, POST /admin/users/edit and POST /admin/users/service-account` on the admin console.

200.description: Whether anything changed, and in `ended` what the global logout ended.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

riscReason.description: RISC account-disabled's `reason` (section 2.2), sent to receivers; omitted when not given (#146).

post.summary: Link a federation partner's subject to a person
post.description:
Adds a `federationLink` — `<relationship> <issuer> <subject>` — to the person's entry, so that the partner of that service-provider-side relationship signs them in when it asserts that subject. The subject is the partner's STABLE identifier for them (OpenID Connect `sub`, a SAML persistent NameID), never a name or an address, and the issuer is the relationship's `fedPeer` when omitted. Refused when another person already carries the link (a subject names one person), for a relationship that is not service-provider side, or for a subject that cannot be written. A console administrator is still refused at the sign-in unless the relationship sets `fedMayAssertAdministrators`. The person's links are `federationLinks` (paged by `federationLinksPage`) on `GET /admin-api/users?user=`, and a relationship's are `links` on `GET /admin-api/federation?relationship=`. SCIM sets the same values through the `urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:extension:iya-sts:2.0:User` extension.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/users, POST /admin/users/new, POST /admin/users/edit and POST /admin/users/service-account` on the admin console.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

subject.description: The partner's identifier for the person.

issuer.description: The partner's entity ID or `iss`; the relationship's fedPeer when omitted, and refused if it differs from it.

post.summary: Make an app password for somebody, returned once
post.description:
Generates an APP PASSWORD for the person — twenty-four characters, printed in groups of four — names it, scopes it to one or more of the five password-only doors (`ldap`, `wstrust`, `scim`, `ssf`, `est`), stores a scrypt hash of it on their entry and **returns it ONCE** in `appPassword`. Nothing can show it again.

**What it is for**: in product mode a person who holds a second factor, or of whom one is required, is refused their own password at those five doors, which cannot ask for the second factor; an app password scoped to a door is accepted there instead. It is ONE factor, it is accepted ONLY at the doors it names, and NEVER at the sign-in screen or any browser sign-in. A disabled account refuses it; a password reset leaves it alone.

**Shared Signals**: a CAEP `credential-change` (`password`, `create`) with its name as `friendly_name`.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/users, POST /admin/users/new, POST /admin/users/edit and POST /admin/users/service-account` on the admin console.

200.description: The app password ONCE (`appPassword`), its public four-character `id`, name, doors and when it was made.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

name.description: What it is for — the client it goes in. At most 64 characters, unique among this person's.

doors.description: The doors it is accepted at. At least one.

post.summary: Begin enrolling a passkey for somebody, in your own browser
post.description:
Mints a WebAuthn registration challenge bound to YOU (the access token's subject, which must be a person), the person and the lane, held for five minutes at most and usable once, and answers the ceremony your browser runs (`ceremony`): the challenge, the realm's RP ID, the PERSON's user handle (`user.id`, per lane, #643) with their name and display name (the passkey policy's userDisplayName), the credentials to exclude (the person's keys in that lane) and `options` — the algorithms offered in order and the realm's attestation, user verification, resident key, hints and timeout. Every byte string is base64url.

Refused unless the person's passkey policy's `adminEnrolment` is `on` (STS-AUTHN-0440, off by default), the person is in this realm's directory (STS-AUTHN-0441), the caller is a person (STS-AUTHN-0445), the realm accepts a passkey at all (STS-AUTHN-0531), and the lane and `webauthn.maxKeysPerPerson` allow it. No role is asked: a passkey has none since #1135, and the realm decides at each sign-in how it is used. There is no import of a registration made elsewhere.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/users, POST /admin/users/new, POST /admin/users/edit and POST /admin/users/service-account` on the admin console.

get.summary: Every session this service is holding right now, across the three protocols that have one
get.description:
WHAT IS LIVE, as opposed to what has been ISSUED — which is `GET /admin-api/tokens`, and everything in that list outlives everything in this one.

A session is state THIS SERVICE holds that makes somebody currently authenticated. Three protocols here have one and the other seven do not:

* the **browser sign-on session** from `/authn/login`, which OAuth 2.0 / OIDC, WS-Federation, SAML 2.0, SAML 1.1 and the admin console all share — so one row may be carrying relying parties, realms and service providers at once, and `protocol` says which protocol the sign-in came THROUGH while `carries` says what is riding on it;
* the **Kerberos ticket-granting ticket**, because a TGT is the Kerberos session and a service ticket is one use of it;
* the **LDAP connection**, because RFC 4511 section 4.2 makes a Bind the authorization state of a CONNECTION.

**THE EXPIRY IS WORKED OUT DIFFERENTLY IN EACH AND `expiryRule` SAYS HOW.** A browser session expires at an absolute instant fixed when it was created (`authn.sessionLifetimeS`) and is NOT extended by use; `authn.sessionIdleTimeoutS`, off by default, ends one earlier when it goes unused. A TGT expires at the `endtime` the KDC sealed into the ticket, which nothing can move. An LDAP connection has NO EXPIRY and answers `expiresAt: 0`, which is not an expiry of the epoch.

Every row carries the `key` and `id` that `POST /admin-api/sessions/revoke` takes, and — for a browser session — the `sessionId` that `GET /admin-api/tokens?session=` takes.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/sessions` on the admin console.

200.description: The live sessions, filtered and paged.

400.description: The answer.

post.summary: End one live session
post.description:
The Revoke button on every row of /admin/sessions, driven without a browser. It is `terminate()` with a selection of one — the SAME function a global logout goes through — so it writes the same audit row, honours the same two settings and gives the same refusals.

**IT IS NOT ONE ACT ACROSS THE THREE KINDS AND THE DIFFERENCE MATTERS.** On a browser session it ends that session and everything hanging off it: the relying parties are notified, the refresh tokens issued on it are revoked. On an LDAP row it closes the socket, which the client sees as its connection dropping mid-conversation. On a Kerberos row it does MORE than the row it names — it stamps a sign-out instant on the PRINCIPAL, after which every ticket-granting ticket that principal authenticated before now is refused KDC_ERR_TGT_REVOKED (20), because Kerberos has no per-ticket revocation. It still reaches no service ticket already in a cache: accepting one never contacts this KDC. Every row's `why` says which of the three it is before it is pressed.

A row that names nothing any more — it ended between the read and the write — answers 400 saying so rather than 200 having done nothing, and the whole `terminate()` result is in `result`.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/sessions` on the admin console.

200.description: What was ended, or why it could not be. The whole termination result is in `result`, including `skipped` and `unknown`.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

select.description: Which session, in the form the list gives it as `id`: `session:…`, `ldap:…` or `krb5:…@REALM`. It is the identifier POST /admin-api/logout/selective takes too, because both go through one termination.

get.summary: Everything this service is still holding for one identity, across every protocol family
get.description:
The protocol-independent view of a person's live state. Without `user` it is the FAMILY LIST — what a logout can reach, what it cannot, and why — which is the same prose /logout and /admin/logout print, read off one table in `logout/logout.ts` rather than copied here.

With `user` it is that identity: every browser sign-on session, every relying party, realm and service provider signed into on one, every token still revocable, every outstanding authorization and pre-authorized code, every directory connection bound as them, and the Kerberos sign-out instant.

**The rows that CANNOT be ended are in the reply on purpose** and carry `terminable: false` with a `why`. A SAML assertion already issued, a Kerberos service ticket already in a cache and an X509-SVID already minted cannot be recalled by this service or by a real one — nothing consults the issuer when they are presented — and a reply that omitted them would make a global logout look complete when it is not.

The identity is a QUERY PARAMETER and not a path segment for the reason /admin-api/users gives: the identities here contain the characters a path is made of.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/logout` on the admin console.

post.summary: End everything this service holds for one identity
post.description:
The default a person gets from `POST /logout` with an empty body, driven by name. Every browser sign-on session, every relying party, realm and service provider on one, every revocable token, every outstanding code, every directory connection bound as them, and a Kerberos sign-out instant after which a TGS-REQ carrying an older ticket is refused KDC_ERR_TGT_REVOKED (20).

**What it cannot do is reported rather than skipped.** The reply's `skipped` array names every live thing that survived and says why.

**What it cannot do FROM HERE is different and is also in the reply.** A front-channel logout notification is an iframe in the signed-out person's own browser and a WS-Federation cleanup is an image in it; neither is something this process performs. They come back in `notifications` and `cleanups` so a caller can load them, and `/logout` is the page where a browser does it by itself.

**The back-channel Logout Tokens ARE sent from here** (OpenID Connect Back-Channel Logout 1.0), to every relying party on an ended session that registered a `backchannel_logout_uri` — after this reply, so `backchannel` lists each with the state it has now, nearly always `pending`, and `GET /admin-api/logout` lists where each got to.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/logout` on the admin console.

post.description:
The selective half. `select` carries row ids from the GET — `session:<id>`, `token:<jti>`, `wsfed-rp:<session>|<realm>`, and so on.

**An empty `select` is REFUSED here and is a global logout at `POST /logout`**, which is the one place the two doors differ and is deliberate: an empty selection arriving at this operation is a caller that built a list and got nothing, where an empty body at /logout is a caller asking for everything. Same absence, opposite intent.

Ids are re-resolved against what is live NOW rather than trusted, so an id that has since been redeemed or expired ends nothing and is answered in `unknown` or `skipped` rather than ending something else.

post.summary: Send a dead back-channel Logout Token delivery again
post.description:
A delivery that ended as a DEAD LETTER — refused with 400, refused by the outbound policy, or still failing after `oauth2.backchannelLogoutAttempts` — is queued again as a new generation: a new Logout Token with a new `jti`, a fresh attempt budget, and the client's CURRENT `backchannel_logout_uri`, because the commonest reason to retry is having corrected it. The attempt is made after this reply, claimed like every other, so exactly one node sends it. Refused for a delivery that is not dead, one retention has removed, and a client with no usable address. `GET /admin-api/logout?deliveryState=dead` lists the dead letters.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/logout` on the admin console.

post.description:
Clears the instant a logout stamped on the principal, so a ticket-granting ticket authenticated before it is accepted again.

**DEVELOPMENT MODE ONLY**: product mode refuses it (HTTP 400). **A real KDC has no such operation.** A fresh AS-REQ gets a ticket newer than the instant but does NOT clear it — tickets from before it stay refused, renewals included, until the latest one of them could still be valid. This exists so a test can put a signed-out ticket back into service without restarting the service.

get.summary: Every group in the embedded LDAP directory, or one in full
get.description:
Without `group` it is the list. With it, one group: every attribute it holds, operational ones included, and every member resolved.

Two answers are easy to mistake for failures and are neither. A process with no directory loaded answers 200 with `directory: false`. A group that is not there answers 200 with `found: false`, because a client can delete or rename one through the protocol between one call and the next, and that is the interesting case rather than a routing problem.

A GROUP HERE GRANTS NOTHING, with two exceptions: no endpoint in this service decides anything on a group, and the only two that do are `admin.readGroup` and `admin.writeGroup`, which say who may use the console. A token CAN carry one — `groups.claim` is on by default and puts the subject's groups in every access token, ID Token and SAML assertion — and carrying a fact is not acting on one.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/groups` on the admin console.

post.summary: Put a group in the directory
post.description:
An entry under `ou=groups`, as a `groupOfNames` — so it is counted as a group by BOTH of the rules /admin/groups applies, its placement and its object class, and stays one if a client moves it.

**The name becomes the `cn` AND the RDN**, so it is refused if it carries a character RFC 4514 section 2.4 reserves in a DN (one of `, = + < > # ; " \`) — the same rule a username is refused by, and refused rather than escaped for the same reason: an `ldapadd` can still create such an entry with the escaping written out. A DN sent here is refused too, because what it would create is a group whose name is another group's DN.

**A member that names nothing is WRITTEN, not refused.** This directory does no referential integrity in either direction — deleting a person leaves their DN in every group that listed them — so a create that refused a dangling member would make the state /admin/groups exists to report impossible to produce from this door. They come back in `dangling`.

**An empty group is allowed and RFC 4519 says it should not be** (`member` is MUST on `groupOfNames`). SCIM already creates one; a management API stricter than SCIM about the same store would be two doors disagreeing about what this directory holds.

**IT GRANTS NOTHING.** No endpoint here decides anything on a group. The two that do are `admin.readGroup` and `admin.writeGroup`, and they are granted at POST /admin-api/rbac rather than by creating a group with the right name — though creating one with the right name and adding somebody to it does the same thing, because those two ARE ordinary groups in this directory.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/groups and POST /admin/groups/owners` on the admin console.

200.description: The DN it was created at, the membership values written, and which of them name nothing.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

displayName.description: Accepted for `group`, spelt the way SCIM spells it.

note.description: What the entry's `description` says about why it exists. Defaults to a sentence saying it was created by hand rather than by a directory client.

members.description: Who is in it, as an array of user names or DNs — a group can hold another group, and no user name names one. A form sends one string, split on newlines and commas. A bare name resolves to that person's OWN entry wherever it is, because somebody seeded by a client certificate is at `cn=<name>,ou=users` and a value written in the `uid=` form would dangle beside the entry it meant to name.

mail.description: The group's own email address, its `mail` attribute (#989): where a report definition shared with the group sends its result notices. One address, or omitted.

post.summary: Put somebody in a group that already exists
post.description:
One membership value onto one group. `group` is its `cn` or its whole DN; `member` is a user name or any DN.

**IT IS IDEMPOTENT.** Adding somebody already listed answers `ok: true` with `changed: false` rather than an error, so a script that adds on every run does not fail on its second one. Membership is asked across `member`, `uniqueMember` and `memberUid` together, which is how /admin/groups and the groups claim ask it — an add that could not see a `memberUid` would write a second value for one membership.

**It writes onto `member`** whatever else the entry carries, rather than extending whichever convention the group already uses: this service's groups claim, the console and RFC 4519 all read `member` first, and guessing which of three attributes was meant would be this operation deciding something the caller did not say.

**It does not create the group as a side effect.** A typo in the name would then be a new group rather than an error. And it writes nothing onto the PERSON: `memberOf` is maintained by nothing here — it is not even a standard attribute — and a value written there is one no other door in this service can take away.

**Removing one is not here.** It is an `ldapmodify` or a SCIM `PATCH`, and POST /admin-api/rbac for the two groups that grant the console.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/groups and POST /admin/groups/owners` on the admin console.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

Writes one value of `attribute` — the attribute by which a group names its policy of a kind, `stsPasskeyPolicy` for the passkey policy — onto the group's own entry, or removes it when `policy` is empty. `policy` is `default` or a named policy of that kind this realm holds (STS-LDAP-0195 otherwise); an attribute no kind declares is refused (STS-LDAP-0194). The policy a group names competes for each of its members on precedence with the policy the application names, the policy the person names and the policies their other groups name: the lowest applies, ties by name, else `default`. A named policy a group still names cannot be deleted. `GET /admin-api/groups?group=` lists the attributes and their choices as `policyReferences`. **Idempotent**: the value the group already names answers `changed: false`.

get.summary: Every entry in this realm's directory, paged
get.description:
The whole store, DN by DN, with where each entry came from — `seed`, an LDAP `add`, or an authentication — and every attribute with every value.

IT IS NOT AN LDAP SEARCH. This is the service showing its own store, which is how a caller tells an empty directory from a filter that matched nothing, and it is why the operational attributes are here: a search withholds `createTimestamp` and `modifyTimestamp` unless they are asked for by name (RFC 4511 §4.5.1.8) and this is not a search.

`q` matches the DN, any attribute NAME and any attribute VALUE, case-insensitively — values because the caller who needs this most often has a thumbprint or a secret in hand and no idea which entry carries it.

WHERE THE DIRECTORY IS HELD AS A WINDOW ONTO THE STORE (#616) the counts, the `origin` filter, the order and the page are asked of the store, so the order is the store's key order (`order: key`), and a `q` — which matches values the store holds sealed — looks inside at most a bounded number of entries and says how many in `search`.

THE REPLY IS THIS REALM'S DIRECTORY AND NO OTHER. Since 2026-08-25 each trust realm has a subtree of its own; reach another realm's through its own path prefix.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/ldap/directory` on the admin console.

get.description:
One entry per identifier under `ou=applications`, every attribute on it, and the published SCHEMA — the object classes and every attribute name with what sets it.

THE SCHEMA IS WHY THIS IS NOT `GET /admin-api/applications`. That operation is the registry as the console works with it: the counters, the drill-down, the writes. This is the registry as the DIRECTORY holds it, and the vocabulary is the half a client reading an entry back over 389 actually needs — this directory is schemaless, so an entry carrying thirty invented attribute names is otherwise guesswork.

THESE ENTRIES ARE THE REGISTRY rather than a copy of one. Nothing caches them, so an `ldapmodify` of `oauthRedirectUri` changes which redirect URI RFC 9700 mode accepts on the next request.

Two attributes hold CREDENTIALS in the clear, for the reason the development Kerberos passwords are printed as settings. They are never written to the audit log.

get.description:

Everywhere else an edit changes what this service HANDS OUT; `fedSigningCertificate` decides whose assertions it will BELIEVE and `fedEnabled` turns a partner on.

get.summary: Who may use the admin console, and how the gate is set
get.description:
The two roles — **Admin Read** and **Admin Write** — with every grant, the settings behind the gate, and who the CALLER is (`you`).

The roles are two ORDINARY GROUPS in the embedded LDAP directory (`admin.readGroup`, `admin.writeGroup`), not a store of the console's own. So this resource, `/admin/rbac`, an `ldapmodify` on 389 or 636 and a SCIM PATCH of the group are four doors onto one membership, and a grant made through any of them is visible through all of them.

**WRITE IMPLIES READ.** A member of the write group does not also need the read group.

**The bootstrap administrator** (`admin.bootstrapUsername`, reported in `bootstrap`) is made a member of both groups at startup. In DEVELOPMENT mode, until it first signs in to `/admin` (`bootstrap.claimedAt`), `openToAnyone` is true and anybody who signs in holds both roles; a process that never seeded it (`bootstrap.seeded` false) keeps the older rule: open while NEITHER group has a member. **In PRODUCT mode the window never opens** (`windowOpens` false, `openToAnyone` false whatever `admin.openWhenEmpty` says), and until the bootstrap administrator has claimed the console (`bootstrapPasswordRequired` true) its roles are honoured only from a PASSWORD sign-in through its own realm, which is also the only sign-in that claims it — a federation partner, a certificate, a wallet or a Kerberos ticket naming it holds nothing. `admin.openWhenEmpty` turns the open window off, and `closedToEveryone` reports a console no browser can reach, which is what this resource is the way out of.

`enforced` reports whether the roster decides anything. It is always true now — the console gate became unconditional on 2026-09-06 — and the field is kept because a client reading it should not have to know that.

**EVERY LIST IN THE REPLY IS PAGED.** `grants` by `page` and `per`, with `page`, `pages`, `perPage`, `firstRow`, `lastRow` and `matched` at the top level; `candidates` by `candidatesPage` and the same `per`, answered in `candidatesPaging`. `roles` carries each role's counts (`memberCount`, `presentCount`, `danglingCount`, `claimedCount`) and, since 2026-09-13, not its `members` and `claimed` lists: those were every membership unpaged, and they are the rows `grants` pages — `?role=read` narrows it to one role.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/rbac` on the admin console.

parameters.description: Narrows `candidates` — the people a role could be granted to — to usernames containing this, case-insensitive. Where the directory is held in memory the list is the directory and who has signed in; where it is a window (#359) it is the direct children of ou=users, a page at a time, and a person who has signed in with no entry is not listed (a typed name can still be granted). `candidateSearch` says how many candidates there are in all and how many matched. A windowed search's count stops at `countCap` (100,000, the furthest the pager reaches; #1308): where more match, `matched` is `countCap` and `countCapped` is true — MORE THAN `matched` match, and `candidatesPaging` stops there. Held in memory, the count is exact and `countCapped` is false. `complete` says whether this page holds every one it counted: where it is false, `incomplete` says how many names a DN cannot hold were left out (`unusable`), how many counted rows the page did not reach (`short`, most often two entries sharing one RDN value), and whether the list stops at the walk's cap (`capped`, `cap`).

post.summary: Give somebody a console role
post.description:
Adds them to the role's group as a `member`, creating the group if this is the first grant — which is why "the group does not exist" and "the group has no members" are the same state everywhere in this feature.

**The person must exist.** A name with no entry in this realm's directory is REFUSED with 400, `reason: "noSuchPerson"` and an `errors` sentence naming them, and nothing is written: create them first (POST /admin-api/users/create) and grant the role then. A role is granted only to somebody who exists, so that a person created later under the same name inherits nothing. A name carrying a character RFC 4514 reserves in a DN is refused too — the same refusal `POST /admin-api/users/create` gives, for the same reason.

Granting a role somebody already holds answers 200 with `changed: false` rather than 400, so a script that grants on every run does not fail on its second one.

**THE FIRST GRANT ON A SERVICE CLOSES THE DOOR BEHIND IT.** While the roster is empty anybody who signs in holds both roles; the moment one grant exists, everybody not in one of the two groups is refused at every page of the console. Grant yourself first.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/rbac` on the admin console.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

Removes them from the role's group — from EVERY membership attribute that named them (`member`, `uniqueMember`, `memberUid`) rather than from the first one found, because a person listed twice by two clients would otherwise still hold the role after a revoke that reported success.

Revoking a role somebody does not hold answers 200 with `changed: false`, and so does revoking from a group that does not exist.

**Taking away the LAST grant empties the roster.** Where no bootstrap administrator was seeded that re-opens the console to anybody who signs in, in development mode (or closes it to everybody, if `admin.openWhenEmpty` is off, and always in product mode); once the bootstrap administrator has signed in it closes the console to everybody. The reply says which.

get.summary: Who holds a second factor, and how RFC 6238 is configured here
get.description:
One row per person — this realm's directory people and everybody this service has SEEN, unioned — saying whether they hold a password, how many of their passkeys may sign them in on their own (`primaryKeys`) and may be a SECOND factor (`mfaKeys`), and whether an authenticator app is enrolled. A passkey has no role since #1135: both counts are of the same keys, by what the realm lets a key do, so each is every key the person holds or none.

**TWO MECHANISMS COUNT AS A SECOND FACTOR HERE**: any passkey, where the realm lets one be a second factor, and an RFC 6238 authenticator app. A person holding either is asked for it at the sign-in screen and a password alone will not sign them in; `secondFactor` says which one they will be asked for, and somebody holding both is asked for the key with the code offered as the alternative.

**`totpUsable: false` IS THE ROW TO LOOK FOR.** It means an enrolment exists that this process cannot read — almost always a shared secret sealed under a key-encryption key that has since been rotated. Those people are REFUSED at the code step rather than let through on one factor, so they cannot sign in at all until the enrolment is cleared.

**CODES ARE VERIFIED FOR REAL IN BOTH MODES**, which almost nothing else in this service is. `totp` carries the algorithm table, read from the module that performs the algorithm.

The scan stops at 5,000 people (`capped`), because reading a credential per person happens on the one thread that answers every socket this service holds — the scan, not the count: `counts` is over the capped roster, and `directoryPeople` and `directoryCounts` over every person the directory defines, as on GET /admin-api/users (#610).

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/users` on the admin console.

get.summary: Everything issued, grouped into what came back in one reply
get.description:
One list, newest first, filtered and paged. Claims and facts only — the signed token, the assertion XML and the ticket are never kept, and the `jti` is all any operation here needs.

**AN ENTRY IS ONE ISSUANCE AND NOT ONE CREDENTIAL, since 2026-09-05.** OAuth 2.0 and OIDC are the only families here that hand back several credentials at once — an access token, a refresh token and an ID Token out of one code redemption — so those arrive as one entry in `sets` carrying its `members`. Every other family issues one credential per act, so a SAML assertion, a Kerberos ticket and an SVID are each a set of one.

`issued` is the same credentials flattened out of `sets`, so a caller written against the older per-credential shape reads exactly what it read. What changed under it is the paging: a page is a whole number of replies, so `page`, `pages`, `matched` and `shown` count SETS while `held` and `matchedCredentials` count credentials.

OID4VCI credentials are NOT in this list. They are counted on /admin-api/metrics and listed nowhere, which is a gap rather than a principle and is said here so "everything issued" is read as the four families it says.

post.summary: Disown one assertion, ticket or SVID (RECORD ONLY)
post.description:
**THIS CHANGES NOTHING OUTSIDE THIS SERVICE AND THAT IS NOT A DEFECT.** A relying party validates a SAML assertion's signature and its Conditions and asks nobody; a Kerberos service decrypts a ticket with a key it already holds; an X509-SVID chains to a bundle. None of them will ever consult this service, so the credential goes on working until it expires and the holder is not told.

What it does is record that THIS IDENTITY PROVIDER HAS DISOWNED the credential, which is a different claim and a useful one: it is what a global sign-out can report, what CAEP transmits to a receiver that subscribed, and what SAML Single Logout carries for an assertion issued through a browser profile. A WS-Trust assertion has neither channel and the mark is the whole of what exists for it.

Until 2026-09-05 this was impossible and every surface said so. What changed is the recognition that what this service KNOWS and what a relying party will HONOUR are two claims, and only the second was ever out of reach. Every row of GET /admin-api/tokens carries `revocationReach` to keep them apart.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/tokens` on the admin console.

post.summary: Revoke every revocable credential in one issuance
post.description:
One act instead of one call per credential. It writes NOWHERE NEW: each member goes through the same revocation `/oauth2/revoke` performs, one at a time, into the same set of revoked `jti`s — so a token revoked here immediately introspects as inactive, is refused by UserInfo with `invalid_token`, and fails the refresh grant with `invalid_grant`.

A set holding nothing revocable is REFUSED with 400 rather than answered with "revoked 0": nothing consults this service about a SAML assertion, a Kerberos ticket or an SVID, so a success would be a claim about the world that is not true. That is the same answer `revoke-kind` gives for an unrevocable kind.

get.summary: Every trust realm, its endpoints and what it sets
get.description:
A TRUST REALM is a whole logical copy of this service: its own configuration, its own signing key, and its own sessions, authorization codes, tokens, credential offers, service providers, statistics and audit log — answering on the same sockets as every other realm and told apart by a segment at the front of the path.

The DEFAULT realm has no prefix, cannot be removed and cannot be renamed: every URL this service published before realms existed is a URL in it. A process with no realms defined behaves exactly as it did before this feature existed, which is a property of one predicate rather than a claim.

Each row carries the realm's `domain` and `baseDn`, its `pathPrefix`, its `baseUrl`, the `kid` of its signing key — two realms showing one kid would be two names for one authorization server — the settings it sets, and the four discovery documents a client asks for first.

`retiring` is null, or says the realm is being REMOVED (#262, #294): `since` and `sinceIso`, whether the removal is `inProgress` or was `interrupted` (the process doing it stopped; every new sign-in and issuance in it is refused until it is finished), `refusing`, `why` and `finish` — for an interrupted one, POST /admin-api/realms/remove again, from another realm.

`support` is the part answered nowhere else: WHICH protocol families a realm actually separates, which is not a tidy answer. A realm separates what this service ISSUES and everything it holds while issuing it — keys, sessions, codes, tokens, offers, artifacts, statistics and the audit log. It does NOT separate the embedded directory: LDAP answers on a socket with no path to put a segment in, so there is one set of people, groups and applications for the whole process — which means OAuth client registrations, SAML service provider entries, the SPIFFE registry and the two admin console roles are shared. Kerberos, the certificate the main port and LDAPS 636 present, and SPIFFE's four sockets are shared for the same reason.

`reserved` is the list of ids a realm may not be called, read off the live router: they are the first segments of paths this service already serves, and the refusal stands whatever `realms.pathSegment` is set to precisely so that clearing that setting cannot turn an existing realm into a shadow over the console or the authorization server.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/realms` on the admin console.

post.summary: Define a trust realm
post.description:
Every HTTP endpoint this service has begins answering under the new realm's prefix immediately, with a signing key of its own and nothing issued yet.

The `id` becomes a PATH SEGMENT, so it is lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, starts with a letter or a digit, and is at most 31 characters. It may not be `default`, and it may not be the first segment of a path this service already serves — `GET /admin-api/realms` lists those in `reserved`.

The `domain` is the realm's DNS domain — `iyasec.io` — and it is FIXED from here on. Its directory is a tree of its own at the RFC 2247 mapping of it (`dc=iyasec,dc=io`), no two realms may share one, and one inside another realm's is allowed and is a separate tree. Omitted, it is `<id>.<global.domain>`.

EIGHT SETTINGS ARE SEEDED ON A NEW REALM FROM ITS DOMAIN and they are the ones that are NAMES rather than behaviour: the SAML 2.0 entityID (`urn:<domain>:idp`), the SAML 1.1 providerID (`urn:<domain>:idp:saml11`), the WS-Federation entityID, the WS-Trust issuer and the SAML assertion issuer (`urn:<domain>:sts`), the SPIFFE trust domain (the domain), the Kerberos realm (the domain in capitals), and the OpenID4VP verifier client id (the process's with the id appended). Two realms carrying one entityID is not a configuration choice — it is two identity providers claiming one name, which a service provider is entitled to refuse. They are ORDINARY settings on the realm: pass `overrides` to choose your own, or unset them afterwards to go back to sharing the process's name, which is a case worth being able to build for testing.

The OAuth issuer is deliberately NOT seeded: it defaults to naming the base URL a request arrived on, and that already carries the realm prefix.

Creation is capped by `realms.maxCount`, which counts the default realm. At the cap the create is refused and nothing is defined. Lowering the cap does not remove realms that already exist. Only a service administrator in the default realm may change the limit.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/realms` on the admin console.

200.description: The realm id, in `realm`.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

id.description: Lower-case letters, digits and hyphens. It is the path segment.

name.description: What a person calls it. Free text; defaults to the id.

domain.description: The realm's DNS domain, at least two labels. Fixed once the realm exists; defaults to `<id>.<global.domain>`.

overrides.description: Settings to set on the realm, named by the dot paths GET /admin-api/config lists. They win over the seeded names. Every `realms.*` key is refused on a realm: one of them decides whether realms exist and where they are found, and a realm carrying it would be changing how it was reached half way through the request that found it.

post.summary: Remove a realm, and everything it holds
post.description:
EVERYTHING IT ACCUMULATED GOES WITH IT: its sessions, its authorization codes, its tokens, its refresh families, its credential offers, its service providers, its statistics, its audit log and its signing key. That is deliberate rather than thorough — a realm re-created with the same id inheriting the last one's sessions and tokens would be the single most surprising thing a re-created realm could do.

NOTHING IS REMOVED FROM THE DIRECTORY, because nothing there belongs to a realm: `ou=users`, `ou=groups` and `ou=applications` are shared by every realm in this process.

A realm cannot remove ITSELF — a call to `/realm/acme/admin-api/realms/remove` naming `acme` is refused. Everything about the removal would work; what would not is the caller, which would be talking to a prefix that had stopped existing. Call it from another realm, or from the default one.

The DEFAULT realm cannot be removed at all.

post.description:
A RUNTIME OVERRIDE — the top of config.js's five layers. Whether it outlives the process is `persistence.appconfig`: with a persistent store (`persistence.mode` `ldif` or `postgres`) it is written down and re-applied at the next start through this same function, which is why it adds no sixth layer, and only with `persistence.mode=memory` is it gone on restart. A write made while a non-default realm is ambient lands on that realm and is written down with the realm row, so `persistence.realms` decides it there. The reply's `message` says which. See `GET /admin-api/persistence`.

NOTHING HERE WRITES TO THE APPCONFIG FILE in either mode, and that is deliberate rather than unfinished: a service that edited a file checked into a repository would leave a test's forgotten change behind permanently. The durable copy goes to the persistent store, which is not a place anything is checked in from.

The change applies to the next token, assertion, ticket or search. Nothing already issued changes, because a token is a signed document.

A setting whose `editable` is false is REFUSED with the reason rather than accepted, and a value that does not fit the setting's type is refused by name.

What the console's per-section Save posts, and it is not a convenience: a section is how a person changes configuration, and one call per field would make a partly-applied section the ordinary outcome of a mistake in any one of them.

ALL-OR-NOTHING. Every value is checked before any is written, so a body with one bad field changes nothing and names it. get.summary: The security-key ceremony's settings, and what a key may be here
get.description:
Every `webauthn.*` setting, in four kinds. **THE CEREMONY**: the RP name, the RP ID override, the algorithms offered (with the three flags that widen or narrow them: `insecureAlgorithms`, `pqcOnly` and `pqcAlongsideClassical`), the user verification requirement, the attestation conveyance and the timeout — handed to the browser in the `PublicKeyCredential` options. **CTAP2**: the authenticator attachment and whether `credProps` is asked for; whether the credential is discoverable (a resident key) is the passkey policy's `securityKeyResidentKey` since #527, not a setting here. **POLICY**: whether a key may be a primary credential, whether it may be a second factor, and how many one person may hold — which are not WebAuthn at all but what THIS service does with a key.

**NOT ONE OF THESE EXISTED UNTIL 2026-09-10.** Every ceremony parameter was a literal in a string in `authn/authn.ts`, and this service said there was nothing an operator could usefully turn — true of the cryptography and false of the ceremony.

**ONE IS ENFORCED AND THE REST ARE REQUESTS.** `webauthn.userVerification` is sent to the browser AND checked against the UV flag when the ceremony returns, because that flag is inside the bytes the authenticator signed. get.summary: The KDC's own settings

get.summary: What survives a restart, where it is written, and whether that is working
get.description:
The `persistence.*` settings AND — unlike every other operation in this group — a `status` member saying what the store is actually doing: which mode is in force, whether it FELL BACK to memory because it could not be opened, where it writes, how many entries and realms it holds, when it last wrote, and the error if the last write failed.

THREE THINGS PERSIST when a store is on: the embedded LDAP directory (which is also the applications registry, the federation register and the SPIFFE registry — they are directory entries and nothing else), the trust realm registry, and the runtime appconfig overrides that `POST /admin-api/config/set` writes.

AND, IN PRODUCT MODE ON A POSTGRES STORE SINCE 2026-09-06, WHAT THIS SERVICE MINTS: sessions, access tokens, ID Tokens, refresh tokens, authorization codes, pre-authorized codes, SAML artifacts, Kerberos principals and tickets, the replay caches, the statistics and the audit log — each row encrypted under the same key-encryption key that protects the signing keys, so a dump of the table is not a set of usable credentials. `status.minted` reports it.

IN DEVELOPMENT MODE NONE OF THAT PERSISTS, and the reason is the one the rule always rested on: the signing key is regenerated on every start there, so a token restored from a disk would verify against nothing. Product mode keeps its keys — which is why it requires a store — and that single fact is what makes restoring the rest of it honest. The ldif store holds no minted state in either mode: it writes whole files per flush, which is right for a directory somebody types into and wrong for a session table that changes on every request.

PROCESSES AGAINST ONE POSTGRES STORE COORDINATE SINCE 2026-09-06, and this paragraph said the opposite before it. Every change is written to a monotonic log inside the transaction that made it, and each process applies what the others committed — the directory, the realms, the settings and the minted rows alike. A LISTEN/NOTIFY nudge only makes that prompt: the LOG is the contract, so a missed notification costs latency and never a change. `status.coordinates` and `status.replication` report it; `persistence.coordinate` turns it off.

THE DATABASE PASSWORD NEED NOT BE IN THE CONNECTION STRING SINCE 2026-09-12. `persistence.databasePasswordProvider` reads it from the five places the key-encryption key comes from — a mounted file, AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault — and by default out of the SAME file or secret, told apart by a field. `status.database.passwordFrom` says WHERE it came from and never what it is, which is the rule this whole reply follows about the connection string: the host, port, database and user are parsed out of it and the string itself is never returned.

IT SHARES STATE AND NOT SOCKETS. The KDC, both LDAP listeners, the main port and SPIFFE's four are bound per process. And the replay caches and DPoP jti sets CONVERGE rather than synchronise: between a write in one process and its arrival in another there is a window the size of persistence.pollInterval in which a proof one process refused is accepted by another.

FIVE OF THE SIX SETTINGS ARE RESTART-ONLY, because the store is opened and read before the HTTP listener binds. `persistence.databaseUrl` is never echoed back in `status` — it carries a password, so the host, port, database and user are parsed out of it and reported instead.

get.summary: Whether several nodes against one store behave as one service, and what active-active mode still waits for
get.description:
The five `cluster.*` settings AND a `status` member: this node's resolved mode, identity, heartbeat and leases; a snapshot of every member row and every lease, read by the database clock and at most one heartbeat old (`status.snapshotAgeMs`) — each member row carrying what only that node can say about itself in `nodes[].info` (host, port, pid, `uptimeMs`, the count of processes answering requests there, and `lastStallMs`, the event-loop stall that explains a late heartbeat), which is what the console draws its member list from, and `status.members`, the same rows folded BY NAME as the console draws them (`running` node ids; `restarts`, per running name, how many earlier rows it left and when the last ended; `leftOrExpired`, one row per name with no running member, with `earlierLives`); the capability table active-active mode is held to (`status.self.capabilities`, with `missing` and `acceptedMissing`); where each shared secret's value came from (never the value); and the read barrier's counters.

IN ACTIVE-PASSIVE MODE ONE NODE SERVES and every other node waits before it restores or binds anything, so a standby never answers this operation — what answers is the active node. IN ACTIVE-ACTIVE MODE EVERY NODE SERVES, and a node refuses to start while a capability is missing and not named in `cluster.acceptMissingCapabilities`.

EVERY CLUSTERED WRITE IS FENCED by the node's membership (and in active-passive mode by the service lease's token), and a node that has lost either exits. A node's settings fingerprint is never returned — only whether it agrees with the node answering (`nodes[].agrees`).

get.summary: The TLS certificate's own settings
get.description:
The `tls.*` settings: the hostnames and IP addresses that go into the self-signed certificate this service mints on every start, and what it makes of a CLIENT's.

get.summary: How long an issued assertion is valid, and the clock skew written into it
get.description:
The two assertion lifetimes — SAML 2.0 and SAML 1.1 — and the clock skew added to BOTH ENDS of each, which is what this service writes into `Conditions/NotBefore` and `NotOnOrAfter`, beside the signing, NameID, artifact and SAML 2.0 encryption choices and the WS-Federation assertion lifetime — sixteen settings in all.

get.description:

get.description:

**A UserInfo response is built on EVERY call.** An access token, an ID Token and both SAML assertions are signed documents: a claim added to one of those sets reaches a client at its next sign-in and never reaches what it already holds. post.summary: Set which LDAP attributes one set carries
post.description:
The array REPLACES the selection for that set. An attribute not in the array is removed, which is how removal is expressed — there is no per-attribute remove, because the console's control is a table of checkboxes and an API that removed differently would be a second model of the same state.

The value a selected attribute carries is the one on that person's entry under ou=users, or — where the entry has nothing — invented from their username, deterministically, so one username is one invented person across restarts. Unlike POST /admin-api/credential-claims/select this does NOT sweep the directory: the credential page writes the attributes it needs onto every entry, and doing it from here as well would mean two pages racing to populate one directory. Selecting an attribute nobody has an entry value for still produces a claim; it is generated, and `attributeReport` says so per claim.

An unknown attribute name refuses the WHOLE call rather than being skipped: the catalogue is fixed, so an unknown name is either a hand-written request that deserves an answer or a rename that left a caller behind. `attributeCatalogue` in the GET beside this is the list — and it is ONE catalogue for all four sets, so either GET answers it in full.

A TYPED claim of the same name WINS over one of these, and THE PROTOCOL'S OWN beats both — which is worth knowing before it is discovered on the wire. An ID Token always carries name, given_name, family_name, preferred_username and email built from the sign-in, so selecting cn, givenName, sn, uid or mail ON THAT SET changes nothing the client sees; the same five reach an access token from the directory, because the protocol sets none of them there. A SAML 2.0 assertion sets `name` the same way and a WS-Federation one sets the whole identity claim list. Both halves are reported by that same GET.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/userinfo-claims` on the admin console.

200.description: What the set carries now, in `attributes`, with `added` and `removed`.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

attributes.description: LDAP attribute type names, from `attributeCatalogue`. An EMPTY array clears the selection — and so does an ABSENT one, so a misspelt field name empties the set rather than being refused. The reply names everything it `removed` and the audit log keeps a row saying the same, and `attributes-clear` is how a caller that means it says so.

get.summary: The custom attributes every new SAML assertion will carry
get.description:
The two SAML sets — SAML 2.0 Attribute and SAML 1.1 Attribute (WS-Federation) — with the rules that govern them. The 2.0 set reaches every assertion WS-Trust issues with a 2.0 token type; the 1.1 set reaches the 1.1 ones, which is what WS-Federation's passive requestor profile carries, so the 1.1 half is the one a browser sign-in exercises.

Each set has TWO HALVES and they are configured by different operations. `claims` are TYPED: a name and a value somebody wrote, the same for everybody except where a ${placeholder} carries the sign-in. `attributes` are LDAP ATTRIBUTE TYPES chosen from `attributeCatalogue`, whose value is read off that person's entry under ou=users — so an `ldapmodify` changes the next assertion, and an LDAP client and a SAML relying party pointed at this service are shown the same person.

THERE IS NO `reservedJwtClaims` HERE and the absence is the answer rather than an omission: that list is enforced for a JWT set only, because an assertion attribute called `exp` collides with nothing. `defaultSaml11Namespace` is the rule that IS this family's — the namespace a 1.1 attribute gets when the call does not name one.

The two JWT sets are at GET /admin-api/claims. One store behind both, and one audit row per change whichever door made it.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/saml2` on the admin console.

The reply also carries `protocolEndpoints`: every endpoint of this family in the realm the call arrived in, as `{ name, methods, url }` (plus `route` for an HTTP endpoint, `transport` for a socket, and `registered: false` for a route the router no longer has).

get.summary: The claims a Kerberos ticket's PAC carries
get.description:
The `kerberos-pac` claim set — the claims this realm's KDC writes into PAC_CLIENT_CLAIMS_INFO ([MS-PAC] 2.11) while `krb5.pacClaims` is on — with each row's claim id, the four PAC claim types and the claims one person's next TGT would carry, built by the function the KDC calls.

A TGT carries this set, with the person's realm-wide roles under it as a string claim. A service ticket carries what its TGT carried, with the rows of the application whose krb5ServicePrincipalName names the service added and winning by name (that application's Configuration tab, `krb5ClaimsPac`). A claim id is `ad://ext/<name>:<hex>`, the hex derived from the name (`idFormat`). Nothing already issued changes.

The set's TICKED CATALOGUE (#498) is the other pages' `attributeCatalogue` (each row with the `pacClaimId` it becomes) and `sets[].attributes`: a ticked attribute is a string claim of every value on the person's entry, under the rows and the roles claim, which win by claim id. `preview.byLdap` is what each attribute would carry for the person.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/kerberos` on the admin console.

The reply also carries `protocolEndpoints`: every endpoint of this family in the realm the call arrived in, as `{ name, methods, url }` (plus `route` for an HTTP endpoint, `transport` for a socket, and `registered: false` for a route the router no longer has).

200.description: The PAC set, its claim ids, the setting and the preview.

parameters.description: Whose claims to preview: `preview.claims` is what their next TGT would carry.

post.summary: Start an OpenID4VP verification: build a request for a wallet
post.description:
Builds a presentation request — the one door a verification starts at since #594 — and answers how a wallet is handed it: `walletUrl` (what a same-device start redirects to: the web wallet `wallet` named or `oid4vp.walletUrl` configures, with the request on its query, or — with neither, the default — the same as `requestUri`), `requestUri` (the request under the scheme a wallet app registers for: `openid4vp://`, HAIP's `haip-vp://` where `oid4vp.walletInvocation` says so, or SIOPv2's `siopv2://` for an ID Token alone; what a cross-device QR code carries), `wallet` (the address or scheme before the query), `query` itself, and — by reference — the `request_uri` the wallet fetches the signed Request Object from. `state` names it; `GET /verifications?state=` reads its outcome.

The body names what the page's query names, every member optional: `format` (a format id, `GET /verifier-request` lists them; the configured default when absent), `by` (`value` or `reference`), `client_id_prefix` (a signed request's Client Identifier Prefix — naming one asks for a request by reference), `response_type`, `response_mode`, `mode` (`same-device` or `cross-device`, which only says which of the two addresses a caller means to use) and `wallet` (held to `oid4vp.walletUrl` and `oid4vp.allowedWalletUrls` wherever only registered addresses are accepted).

`redirect_uri` (#594) is the caller's own page the Response Endpoint sends the wallet to once it has answered (OpenID4VP 1.0 section 8.2). Wherever only registered addresses are accepted it must be one of the CALLING CLIENT's registered redirect URIs, matched whole (400, STS-VC-0123); left off, the Response Endpoint answers no `redirect_uri` — what a wallet on another device wants.

What the request ASKS FOR is the Verifier request's configuration (`/verifier-request`), frozen onto the transaction now. Refused as the page refuses: 400 for what the request names wrongly (STS-VC-0032) and for a wallet this realm will not send a request to (STS-VC-0033), and 500 with the builder's own code where no request can be built — a Verifier Attestation this realm cannot use (STS-VC-0092), an x509 Client Identifier with nothing to certify (STS-VC-0110 to STS-VC-0113). Answered in every mode: this is an administrator asking.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/vc#vc-tab-verifier-request` on the admin console.

200.description: `state`, `walletUrl`, `requestUri`, `query`, the `request_uri` by reference, and what was asked: `ok`, `message`, `state`, `nonce`, `mode`, `format`, `responseType`, `responseMode`, `byReference`, `clientId`, `requested`, `dcql_query`, `expiresAt`, `wallet`, `walletUrl`, `requestUri`, `query`, `redirectUri` ('' for none) and, by reference, `request_uri`.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

format.description: A format id: dc+sd-jwt, jwt_vc_json, ldp_vc, mso_mdoc. Not a closed set here, as on `/verifier-request/format`: a form-encoded `+` arrives as a space and is put back, and the Verifier refuses anything else by name.

wallet.description: A web wallet to send the holder to, if not `oid4vp.walletUrl` or a wallet app (the default).

redirect_uri.description: The caller's page the wallet is sent to once the Verifier has answered (#594); a registered redirect URI of the calling client wherever only registered addresses are accepted.

get.summary: Every federation relationship, in either direction
get.description:
This service can be EITHER END of a federation relationship, in five protocols: SAML 2.0, SAML 1.1, WS-Federation 1.2, OpenID Connect and OAuth 2.0.

**This is the one feature here that has to be configured before it will do anything.** Everywhere else this service accepts what it is given — any username, any client_id, any entityID, any LDAP bind. It cannot do that at an assertion consumer service: what arrives there is an unauthenticated HTTP request claiming to be a person, and the session it produces is the same one `/oauth2/authorize`, `/wsfed`, `/saml2` and the admin console all read. So a relationship is created DISABLED, and an assertion is refused unless it verifies against the certificate configured on it.

**And the gate is on the SUBJECT too (#109).** A partner signs in only the person its (issuer, subject) is linked to — a `federationLink` on the entry — and what happens to a subject nobody linked is the relationship's `fedSubjectPolicy`: a local sign-in as the person it names before linking (`link-at-first-sign-in`, the default), a refusal (`pre-linked`), a new namespaced entry (`jit-namespaced`), or, in development only, the old name match (`any-existing`). `fedSubjectGroup`, `fedSubjectDomain` and `fedSubjectPattern` narrow it further, and a console administrator is refused unless `fedMayAssertAdministrators` is on.

`?relationship=<id>` returns one of them, with everything it holds and the URLs to configure at the partner. It answers 200 with `found: false` for an id that is not registered.

This resource holds nothing: every row is an entry under `ou=federations`, the same one an `ldapsearch` reads.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/federation` on the admin console.

The reply also carries `protocolEndpoints`: every endpoint of this family in the realm the call arrived in, as `{ name, methods, url }` (plus `route` for an HTTP endpoint, `transport` for a socket, and `registered: false` for a route the router no longer has).

post.summary: Register a federation relationship
post.description:
It is created **DISABLED**, whatever this request says, and nothing about it does anything until `enable` is called. That is the one place this operation overrides its input, and it is deliberate: a partner that half-exists and silently accepts assertions is the failure this whole register is arranged to prevent, so enabling is a second act that says the configuration is finished.

**ONE RELATIONSHIP IS ONE DIRECTION.** A partner this service both consumes from and asserts to is two relationships with two ids, because everything that configures one differs by direction.

The reply carries `readiness.missing` — the fields this protocol and role still need — so a caller can go straight on to `set` for each of them without knowing the schema in advance.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/federation` on the admin console.

200.description: The relationship as created, and what it still needs before it can be enabled usefully.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

id.description: The key, the RDN and a URL segment. It has to start with a letter or a digit and hold only letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore, up to 63 characters.

role.description: Which end THIS SERVICE is. `service-provider` means a foreign identity provider authenticates the person and this service consumes what it issues.

protocol.description: The protocol the relationship runs in. `ssf` (#374) is a partner that signs nobody in and only sends Shared Signals; it takes the service-provider role.

name.description: What to call the partner on a page. The id is the name when this is omitted.

peer.description: The partner's own identifier — a SAML entityID, an OpenID Connect issuer, a WS-Federation wtrealm. On a service-provider-side relationship it is CHECKED: an assertion whose issuer is not this string is refused even when the signature verifies.

application.description: On an identity-provider-side relationship only: the identifier of the partner's entry in `ou=applications`. Its entityID, redirect URIs and certificate stay THERE, where every protocol module reads them — this register holds a pointer and not a copy.

provider.description: A CONSUMER OR SOCIAL PROVIDER (#565): the profile the relationship is made from. Its endpoints, issuer, scope and token authentication are written onto the relationship, `role` must be `service-provider` and `protocol` the profile's (both are in `consumerProviders` on `GET /admin-api/federation`), and the realm must have `federation.consumerProviders` on.

clientId.description: With `provider`: this service's client_id at the provider, set as `fedClientId` in the same act.

clientSecret.description: With `provider`: this service's secret at the provider, set as `fedClientSecret` in the same act and sealed as that field always is. Never echoed.

post.description:
The field must be one of this relationship's — a field belonging to the other ROLE is refused by name rather than written and ignored, and so is one that records what HAPPENED (the counters, the last error).

`fedId`, `fedRole` and `fedProtocol` are refused too, and that is a third category rather than an oversight: they are the relationship's identity, and changing one would leave a SAML relationship carrying a token endpoint. Delete it and make another — there is no state to lose but the counters.

`GET /admin-api/federation?relationship=<id>` returns `editable`, which is exactly the list this operation accepts, so a caller need not guess.

**`fedAttributeMap`** is written `<incoming name>=<LDAP attribute>` and is split at the FIRST equals sign — which matters, because an incoming name can be a URL and a URL can hold one. It is only needed for a partner's own inventions: the ordinary OpenID Connect claims, the SAML `urn:oid:` names and the AD FS claim URIs are mapped already.

**`fedRelease`** names an attribute or claim released to that partner, and it can only REMOVE — from what /admin/claims, /admin/saml-attributes and the groups claim would add, and from nothing else. It cannot touch `sub`, `iss`, `exp` or a NameID. **NO VALUES MEANS NO POLICY, not release nothing**: adding the first value here is what starts the filtering.

get.summary: Every SAML 2.0 service provider, and the endpoints each is configured from
get.description:
A full SAML 2.0 identity provider: HTTP Redirect, HTTP POST and HTTP POST SimpleSign for the AuthnRequest, and HTTP POST, HTTP Redirect, HTTP POST SimpleSign or HTTP Artifact for the Response, with a SOAP artifact resolution service behind the last.

**Every service provider gets its own identity provider metadata** — a distinct entityID and its own endpoints — and **in development a document is minted for any entityID asked for**, so nothing has to be provisioned before a service provider can be pointed at this service; in product every per-service-provider path is a 404 for an entityID that is not registered. That is why `metadataUrl` is on every row rather than being one constant.

This resource holds nothing: every row is an entry in `ou=applications`, the same one `GET /admin-api/applications` reports.

`?sp=<entityID>` returns one of them, with what has been recorded about it — and answers 200 with `found: false` for an entityID that is not registered — whose metadata is still served and whose AuthnRequest would still be answered, in development only.

The list reply carries `mdqRefused`: the entityIDs a request asked the Metadata Query responder to register and product mode refused (no trust anchor, or an answer that did not verify), newest first, paged by `mdqRefusedPage`.

The `?sp=` reply also says what checking its requests' signatures found (`lastRequestVerification`), what they are verified against (`signingCertificates`), the certificate a request carried that nobody has confirmed (`observedSigningCertificate`), whether signed requests are required of it and why (`signedRequestsRequired`), and everything consuming its metadata registered (`metadata`).

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/saml2` on the admin console.

The reply also carries `protocolEndpoints`: every endpoint of this family in the realm the call arrived in, as `{ name, methods, url }` (plus `route` for an HTTP endpoint, `transport` for a socket, and `registered: false` for a route the router no longer has).

200.description: The service providers with the paging that found them, or one of them with its endpoints and its record.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Part of a service provider's entityID, case-insensitive, narrowing the list.

parameters.name: sp
parameters.description: One service provider, by its entityID.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: Which page of the match to return. CLAMPED rather than refused: a page past the end returns the last one, and the reply says which page it actually is.

parameters.name: per
parameters.description: Rows per page. Defaults to 50 and is capped at 300. On a drill-down it is SHARED by every list in the reply, which each carry a page number of their own.

parameters.name: mdqRefusedPage
parameters.description: Which page of `mdqRefused` to return, answered by `mdqRefusedPaging`. The Metadata Query lookups refused in product mode (#112), newest first.

post.summary: Replace the certificates this service provider's signatures are verified against
post.description:
**THE TRUST ANCHOR FOR THIS SERVICE PROVIDER'S SIGNATURES** (2026-09-17). A signed AuthnRequest, LogoutRequest or LogoutResponse from it is VERIFIED against `samlSigningCertificate` in every mode, and refused when it verifies against none — never against the certificate the request carries. The attribute is a LIST (a metadata rollover publishes two keys); this REPLACES it with the one certificate given, and an empty `value` clears it. Consuming the service provider's metadata writes the same list.

Base64 DER or PEM — the armour and whitespace are stripped, because what the attribute holds is what a `ds:X509Certificate` carries. A value that is not a certificate whose key makes an XML signature this service verifies (RSA, EC, EdDSA, DSA, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) is refused and nothing changes: an unusable certificate would make every signature from this service provider fail. Public key material, worth nothing to whoever reads the directory.

post.summary: Consume a service provider's metadata document
post.description:
The same CONSUMPTION `POST /admin-api/applications/refresh-metadata` performs on a fetched document, for a document given here — a service provider whose metadata this service cannot reach. It REGISTERS what the `<md:SPSSODescriptor>` says: every AssertionConsumerService (binding, location, index, isDefault) as a return address — an AuthnRequest is then answered only at one of them, by index, by URL or by default, in every mode — every SingleLogoutService, every signing certificate (`use="signing"` or no `use`) as what its requests are verified against, the encryption certificate, its NameIDFormats (a NameIDPolicy naming another is then InvalidNameIDPolicy), and AuthnRequestsSigned and WantAssertionsSigned. The EFFECTIVE validUntil (earliest in the chain) is enforced — past it every request from the service provider is refused — and past the cacheDuration a document with a URL is fetched again in the background. An EntitiesDescriptor is read for this entity. The protocol URI is selected from the application declaration: SAML 1.1 is selected only for an entry declared for `saml11` and not `saml2`; SAML 2.0 remains the choice for SAML 2.0, dual-protocol and undeclared entries unless `family` explicitly selects one declared SAML family. This operation can therefore consume SAML 1.1-only metadata as well.

REFUSED, changing nothing, for: a document that is not an EntityDescriptor (or an aggregate holding exactly one for this entity) with the selected SPSSODescriptor; an entityID that is not this service provider's; a validUntil already passed; an encryption certificate this service cannot encrypt to; a signature that does not verify against `samlSpMetadataSigningCertificate` or a realm trust anchor when any is set (or no signature then); and a document over `saml2.spMetadataMaxBytes`. A signing certificate no XML signature method uses is skipped and named in `skipped`.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/saml2` on the admin console.
