post.summary: Set the passkey policy profile
post.description:
Writes `cn=default,ou=passkeyPolicies` in this realm's directory, REPLACING what is there; a realm with no entry of its own follows the default realm's. `allowUsernameless` (on by default) offers a passkey sign-in with no username. `requireUsernameless` (off, #608) makes it the only way in for an application whose named authentication policy (`appAuthnPolicy`) lists `webauthn` alone as its first factor: no username field, and a sign-in naming a person refused; it needs `allowUsernameless`, and the `default` profile never applies it to the admin console, the debugger or the user portal. While it is off, "Use a security key" asks the authenticator for a discoverable credential (`residentKey: required`), as "Create a passkey" always does; while it is on, it asks `securityKeyResidentKey` (`discouraged`, `preferred` or `required`, default `required`). `backupEligibility` (`allow` by default) set to `disallow` refuses a synced (backup-eligible) passkey at registration and at sign-in. `enforcePinLength` (off) asks a key for its minimum PIN length (CTAP 2.1 minPinLength) and holds it to `minPinLength` (4 to 63); `pinLengthOnlyIfSupported` (off) accepts a key that does not report. `enforceAttestationAtSignIn` (off) holds every passkey sign-in to the attestation rules in force. `passkeyHints`, `securityKeyHints` and `signInHints` are the WebAuthn hints each ceremony sends, in order, or `none`. `enterpriseSerialAttribute` (empty) names the attribute of a person's entry holding their security-key serials, which a registration's trusted enterprise attestation must name. `userDisplayName`, `rpNameExtras` and `credentialLabel` are the names a passkey prompt and a new key show. `aggregateDevices` (on) offers a person's passkeys as one sign-in choice; off, one per passkey. `postQuantumRequired` (`off`, #718) set to `sign-in` lets only a post-quantum (ML-DSA) passkey sign a person in, as the first credential or the second factor, and `registration-and-sign-in` refuses a classical one at registration too; refused while the realm offers no ML-DSA (STS-AUTHN-0357). `attestationAlgorithms` (`none`, #941, optional) lists the algorithms a passkey's ATTESTATION must be signed with, statement and every certificate leaf to anchor: `post-quantum`, `ml-dsa-44`, `ml-dsa-65`, `ml-dsa-87`, `slh-dsa`, `composite-ml-dsa`; set, it demands a trusted statement and refuses any other at registration (STS-AUTHN-0411), and at sign-in while `enforceAttestationAtSignIn` is on (STS-AUTHN-0412). `postQuantumAllowCredentials` (`realm`, #946; optional) chooses how the passkey step names the keys while one is required: `narrow` the post-quantum ones only, `list-and-refuse` every one, a classical assertion then refused after the ceremony with a page saying why, and `realm` the realm's webauthn.postQuantumAllowCredentials. `registrationAlgorithms` (`realm`, #940; optional) is the ordered list a registration offers this profile's people in place of the realm's webauthn.algorithms, and `registrationMode` (`realm`, #940; optional) is `pq-only` (ML-DSA only, no classical retry), `pq-first` (ML-DSA, then the classical algorithms, whatever the realm's pqcOnly), `classical-only` (no ML-DSA, no post-quantum lane) or `realm` (webauthn.pqcOnly and webauthn.pqcAlongsideClassical); a passkey outside what the profile offers is refused at registration (STS-AUTHN-0432). `clientRules` (empty, #1112; optional) names the clients — `<browser> on <system>`, each a family or `*` with an optional major-version range, `;` between rules — whose registrations offer the list less ML-DSA, where a classical passkey is allowed. Refused: `classical-only` with `postQuantumRequired` not `off` or with `attestationAlgorithms` set (STS-AUTHN-0430), and `pq-only` or `pq-first` where the list offered names no ML-DSA (STS-AUTHN-0431).

**Every field is required** and one left out is refused by name rather than reset to a default, because a save that quietly loosened a rule nobody mentioned is the mistake nobody sees.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/policies` on the admin console.

200.description: The profile now in force and the rules as sentences.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

profile.description: Which profile: `default`, or a named profile (lower-case letters, digits and hyphens), which is created by its first save.

description.description: What the profile is for, for the next person. Optional.

precedence.description: A named profile only: the lowest matching precedence wins. Default 100.

allowUsernameless.description: ON BY DEFAULT. On, the sign-in screen offers *Sign in with a passkey* and the username field's autofill, which ask the browser for any discoverable credential of this realm (WebAuthn Level 3 section 5.4, `allowCredentials` empty) and sign in the account its user handle names, with user verification required and checked. Off, neither is offered and a sign-in always names the person first. Replaces the setting webauthn.usernameless. (`true`/`false`, or `TRUE`/`FALSE` from a form.) Default true.

requireUsernameless.description: OFF BY DEFAULT. On, an application whose authentication mechanism is a passkey and nothing else (the authentication policy it names, appAuthnPolicy, lists `webauthn` alone) gets a sign-in screen with no username field: *Sign in with a passkey* is the way in, and a sign-in that names a person is refused. It needs the row above. The realm's `default` profile does not apply it to the admin console, the debugger or the user portal; a named profile selecting that application does. (`true`/`false`, or `TRUE`/`FALSE` from a form.) Default false.

securityKeyResidentKey.description: The `residentKey` an enrolment through *Use a security key* (or one that names no kind) sends WHILE usernameless sign-in is ON. While it is off the button always asks `required`, so it makes a discoverable credential as *Create a passkey* does (which asks `required` always). `discouraged` or `preferred` spare a security key's few resident slots, at the cost of a key that needs the username to sign in. Replaces the setting webauthn.residentKey. Default `required`.

backupEligibility.description: `allow` (the default) accepts any passkey. `disallow` accepts only DEVICE-BOUND ones: a passkey whose authenticator says it may be backed up or synced (the BE flag, WebAuthn Level 3 section 6.1) is refused when it is registered and when it signs somebody in, so a synced passkey enrolled before the realm said no stops working too. BE never changes for a credential. Default `allow`.

enforcePinLength.description: OFF BY DEFAULT. On, registration asks the authenticator for its minimum PIN length (CTAP 2.1 section 12.4, the minPinLength extension), records it on the key, and refuses a key whose minimum is below the next row, at registration and at every sign-in. A key answers only for relying parties it was configured to tell (CTAP 2.1 setMinPINLength with this RP ID); every other key, and every platform or synced passkey, does not report, and is refused unless the row after next is on. (`true`/`false`, or `TRUE`/`FALSE` from a form.) Default false.

minPinLength.description: The shortest PIN a security key may be set to accept, as the key itself reports it, while the row above is on. Between 4 (CTAP 2.1's own floor) and 63. Between 4 and 63. Default 4.

pinLengthOnlyIfSupported.description: OFF BY DEFAULT, which is the strict reading: while the PIN length is enforced, a key that does not report it is refused. On, such a key is accepted and only a reported minimum is held to the rule — so the rule then binds only keys configured to report to this relying party. (`true`/`false`, or `TRUE`/`FALSE` from a form.) Default false.

enforceAttestationAtSignIn.description: OFF BY DEFAULT. The attestation rules (the webauthn.attestation* settings: the policy, the AAGUID list, the certification level and FIPS) are checked when a passkey is registered. On, they are checked again at every sign-in against what was recorded then and the FIDO Metadata Service as it is now, so a key registered before a rule was tightened, or whose model was since reported compromised, stops signing anybody in. A key with no trusted attestation fails every rule that demands one. (`true`/`false`, or `TRUE`/`FALSE` from a form.) Default false.

postQuantumRequired.description: `off` (the default) accepts a passkey whatever its signature algorithm. `sign-in` accepts only a POST-QUANTUM passkey, one whose algorithm is ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 or ML-DSA-87 (RFC 9964), when it signs somebody in, as the first credential or as the second factor; a classical one may still be registered. `registration-and-sign-in` refuses a classical one at registration too, and enrolment then offers only ML-DSA. The algorithm decides, not the lane a key was created in. Refused while the realm offers no ML-DSA (webauthn.algorithms names none, and neither webauthn.pqcOnly nor webauthn.pqcAlongsideClassical is on). Default `off`.

postQuantumAllowCredentials.description: `realm` (the default) follows the realm's webauthn.postQuantumAllowCredentials. Read only while postQuantumRequired requires a post-quantum passkey at sign-in. `narrow` names only the person's post-quantum (ML-DSA) passkeys in the passkey step's request, so a classical one is never offered, and a person whose device holds only their classical one sees the platform's own "no passkey found" message. `list-and-refuse` names every passkey they hold and refuses a classical one after the ceremony, with a page saying that this application requires a post-quantum passkey and where to add one; the person may then pick a passkey that will be refused. A person holding no post-quantum passkey is told before any ceremony either way. Left out of a save, `realm` is kept. Default `realm`.

registrationAlgorithms.description: `realm` (the default) offers the realm's webauthn.algorithms. Otherwise the signature algorithms a passkey registration offers to this profile's people, in order of preference (an authenticator makes the first it supports), from the algorithms webauthn.algorithms may name. The next row may narrow or reorder it, and a passkey whose algorithm is not one this profile offers is refused when it is registered. Left out of a save, `realm` is kept. An ordered, comma-separated list of ML-DSA-87, ML-DSA-65, ML-DSA-44, EdDSA, ES256, RS256, ESP256, Ed25519, ESP384, ES384, ESP512, ES512, Ed448, ES256K, PS256, PS384, PS512, RS384, RS512, or `none`. Default `realm`.

registrationMode.description: `realm` (the default) follows webauthn.pqcOnly and webauthn.pqcAlongsideClassical. `pq-only` offers only ML-DSA, and refuses a retry with the classical algorithms. `pq-first` offers ML-DSA first and the classical algorithms after it, even where the realm requests ML-DSA only. `classical-only` offers no ML-DSA and no post-quantum passkey beside a classical one, for people whose devices fail an ML-DSA registration. Refused with postQuantumRequired other than off or with attestationAlgorithms set (classical-only), and where the algorithms offered name no ML-DSA (pq-only, pq-first). Left out of a save, `realm` is kept. Default `realm`.

lanes.description: `realm` (the default) follows webauthn.pqcAlongsideClassical. `both` gives this profile's people a classical and a post-quantum passkey side by side, each under its own user handle, wherever the realm's setting is off; `one` gives them one lane wherever it is on. webauthn.pqcOnly still means one lane. Refused as `both` with registrationMode classical-only. Left out of a save, `realm` is kept. Default `realm`.

clientRules.description: EMPTY BY DEFAULT: every client is offered the list as it stands. Otherwise up to 20 rules separated by `;`, each `<browser> on <system>`, where either side is a family as the passkey ceremony rows name it (`Chrome`, `Firefox`, `macOS`, `Android`) or `*` for any, optionally followed by a major-version range (`141`, `130-140`, `130-`, `-140`): `Firefox 140- on Linux; * on Android 13`. A passkey registration from a matching client offers the list less ML-DSA (ES256 and RS256 where that leaves none). Not applied where a classical passkey is not allowed — registrationMode pq-only, webauthn.pqcOnly, postQuantumRequired registration-and-sign-in, or at the sign-in step under postQuantumRequired sign-in — nor to the post-quantum lane, and the ceremony row says it was not. Left out of a save, empty is kept. Default empty.

passkeyHints.description: The WebAuthn hints (Level 3 section 5.4.8) the portal's *Create a passkey* sends, in order, from security-key, client-device and hybrid, or none. They tell the browser which way of making the passkey to lead with. A hint may not contradict webauthn.authenticatorAttachment: client-device implies platform, security-key and hybrid cross-platform. An ordered, comma-separated list of security-key, client-device, hybrid, or `none`. Default `client-device,hybrid`.

securityKeyHints.description: The hints *Use a security key* sends, in order, or none. The button asks for a cross-platform authenticator, so client-device contradicts it and is refused. An ordered, comma-separated list of security-key, client-device, hybrid, or `none`. Default `security-key`.

signInHints.description: The hints a sign-in ceremony sends — the passkey step, the sign-in with no username and its autofill — in order, or none (the default: the browser offers every way it knows). An ordered, comma-separated list of security-key, client-device, hybrid, or `none`. Default `none`.

enterpriseSerialAttribute.description: EMPTY BY DEFAULT: no serial is checked. Set to an attribute of a person's entry (for example `serialNumber`, which may hold several values), a security key registers only with a TRUSTED enterprise attestation whose certificate names a device serial that is one of that person's values. Needs webauthn.attestation set to enterprise, and the vendor or platform configured to release enterprise attestation to this RP ID; without that the browser sends ordinary attestation and every registration is refused. A directory attribute name, or empty for none. Default empty.

userDisplayName.description: EMPTY BY DEFAULT: the name the sign-in knows, else the username. Otherwise up to six directory attributes in order, separated by commas; a group of attributes separated by spaces (givenName sn) joins their values. The first whose every attribute has a value becomes user.displayName (WebAuthn Level 3 section 5.4.3), with control and direction-changing characters removed and at most 64 characters. The username is always user.name. Default empty.

rpNameExtras.description: `none` (the default) shows webauthn.rpName alone. `realm`, `organisation` or `realm-and-organisation` append the realm's name and/or saml.organizationName, so a person with accounts in several realms can tell the prompts apart. Default `none`.

credentialLabel.description: EMPTY BY DEFAULT: the provider's name, else "Passkey" or "Security key". Otherwise this text, with {provider} and {kind} filled in, at most 60 characters. The person may rename it afterwards, as always. Default empty.

aggregateDevices.description: ON BY DEFAULT: one "Use passkey" step whose request lists every one of the person's passkeys, and the browser offers whichever is present. Off, a person with more than one is shown a choice per passkey, by its name, and the request names only that one. (`true`/`false`, or `TRUE`/`FALSE` from a form.) Default true.

recoveryAssurance.description: `any` BY DEFAULT IN DEVELOPMENT, `not-weaker` IN PRODUCT. Whether a way back into the account that asks for no passkey — a password reset link, an activation link, a recovery code, an emailed code or link — restores access for a person who holds one. `any`: at once. `not-weaker`: the first sign-in after it that is not a passkey sign-in reaches no application; the person registers a passkey that satisfies this policy and signs in with it. `operator-only`: as not-weaker, and the self-service doors (the forgot-password form, a recovery code or an emailed code or link at sign-in) are refused; only an administrator's reset link, generated password or activation link remains. Left out of a save, the built-in default is kept. Default `any`.

attestationAlgorithms.description: `none` BY DEFAULT: an attestation is accepted whatever it is signed with. Otherwise a list from post-quantum, ml-dsa-44, ml-dsa-65, ml-dsa-87, slh-dsa and composite-ml-dsa: a passkey registers only with a TRUSTED attestation that carries a certificate, whose statement signature and the signature on every certificate of its chain, from the leaf to the trust anchor, are each one the list allows (`post-quantum` allows any ML-DSA, SLH-DSA or composite ML-DSA signature). Self and none attestation are refused, having no certificate. With enforceAttestationAtSignIn on, every sign-in holds the passkey to it by what its registration recorded, so a passkey registered before the rule stops working. This is the attestation's algorithm, not the passkey's own (postQuantumRequired). Left out of a save, the built-in default is kept. An ordered, comma-separated list of post-quantum, ml-dsa-44, ml-dsa-65, ml-dsa-87, slh-dsa, composite-ml-dsa, or `none`. Default `none`.

adminEnrolment.description: `off` BY DEFAULT. `on` lets an administrator holding the Admin Write console role enrol a passkey for a person this profile applies to, from the person's page on the console or /admin-api: the registration ceremony runs in the administrator's own browser, against an authenticator they hold (a security key to be handed over, say), under the person's user handle, and is verified exactly as the person's own registration is — attestation, algorithms and this policy's registration rules. Nothing made elsewhere can be imported. The key records which administrator enrolled it and when, and the person is told. Left out of a save, the built-in default is kept. Default `off`.

deviceBoundRequired.description: OFF BY DEFAULT. On, an issuance to an application this profile covers waits until the sign-on session is bound to the browser's key, and is refused when the browser skipped that registration or the wait elapsed without a binding. A session that was never offered registration is not refused by this row. Refused while authn.deviceBoundSessions is off. (`true`/`false`, or `TRUE`/`FALSE` from a form.) Default false.

post.summary: Set the locale policy profile
post.description:
Writes `cn=<profile>,ou=localePolicies` in this realm's directory, REPLACING what is there; a realm with no `default` of its own follows the default realm's, and named profiles are the realm's own. `defaultLocale` (`en`) is a BCP 47 language tag: the language a page falls back to, and mail to a person who names none is written in. `populatePreferredLanguage` (on) gives a person created without a `preferredLanguage` that tag. A named profile carries a `precedence` (1 to 1000, 100 when left out) and lists nothing: an application names it in `appLocalePolicy` and a group in `stsLocalePolicy`, and of those naming one for a page the lowest precedence applies, else `default`. A named profile something names is not deleted (STS-I18N-0014).

**Every field is required** and one left out is refused by name rather than reset to a default, because a save that quietly loosened a rule nobody mentioned is the mistake nobody sees.

description.description: What the profile is for, for the next person. Optional.

precedence.description: A named profile only: the lowest matching precedence wins. Default 100.

defaultLocale.description: A BCP 47 language tag (RFC 5646), such as en, fr-CA or zh-TW. Pages are drawn in it when the request, the person's preferredLanguage, the language chooser and the browser name nothing a catalog answers; dates and numbers are formatted for it even where no catalog does. Mail to a person whose entry names no language is written in it. Replaces the setting mail.defaultLanguage. Default `en`.

populatePreferredLanguage.description: ON BY DEFAULT. A person entry created in this realm without a preferredLanguage (RFC 2798 section 2.7) is given the default language above as one — by the console, the management API, SCIM, a federated or self-service sign-up, or a bulk load. A named profile applies where the application that caused the creation names it, or one of the person's groups does. Existing entries are never rewritten. (`true`/`false`, or `TRUE`/`FALSE` from a form.) Default true.

requiredAttributes.description: The attributes every person in this realm must hold a value of, besides uid, cn and sn, which are always required. A list, or comma-separated. post.summary: Set the post-login activity policy profile
post.description:
Writes `cn=<profile>,ou=postLoginPolicies` in this realm's directory, REPLACING what is there; a realm with no `default` of its own follows the default realm's, and named profiles are the realm's own. **Off by default** (`enabled`). On, a person the profile reaches who is due the `activity` is asked after signing in, before being sent back to the application: `pqc-passkey-migration` asks a person holding a classical passkey and no post-quantum one to register an ML-DSA passkey, and — per `noPasskey` — a person holding none to register one. A passkey has no role (#1135): `noPasskeyRole` is accepted and ignored. Skip puts it off `snoozeDays`; once `graceDays` (0 = never) have passed since the person's first invitation Skip is refused (STS-AUTHN-0474) and the sign-in is held until it is done, and a door that cannot ask for it refuses the sign-in (STS-AUTHN-0473). A named profile carries a `precedence` and nothing else: a group names it in `stsPostLoginPolicy` (`POST /admin-api/groups/set-policy`) and an application in `appPostLoginPolicy` (`POST /admin-api/applications/set`). Of the profile the application signed in to names and those the person's groups name the lowest `precedence` wins, so a named profile with `enabled` off excludes them; a started activity's mail and the progress report know no application and select by the groups alone. A profile something names is not deleted (STS-AUTHN-0543). `method` (#1100) is how a classical passkey is migrated: `upgrade` (proved once, then replaced in place on its authenticator), `alongside` (an ML-DSA passkey beside it) or `automatic` (the lanes decide). `attestation` (#1102): `post-quantum` counts an ML-DSA passkey as migrated only where its recorded attestation is post-quantum too. `noPasskeyFallback` (#1103): `classical` offers a person with no passkey a classical retry where their device cannot make ML-DSA.

**Every field is required** and one left out is refused by name rather than reset to a default, because a save that quietly loosened a rule nobody mentioned is the mistake nobody sees.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/policies` on the admin console.

200.description: The profile now in force and the rules as sentences.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

profile.description: Which profile: `default`, or a named profile (lower-case letters, digits and hyphens), which is created by its first save.

description.description: What the profile is for, for the next person. Optional.

precedence.description: A named profile only: the lowest matching precedence wins. Default 100.

enabled.description: OFF BY DEFAULT. On, every person this profile reaches who is due the activity below is asked to do it after signing in, before they are sent back to the application. A named profile with this off EXCLUDES whoever it is selected for: the members of the groups naming it, and a sign-in to an application naming it. (`true`/`false`, or `TRUE`/`FALSE` from a form.) Default false.

activity.description: What is asked. pqc-passkey-migration: a person holding a passkey made with a classical algorithm is asked to register a post-quantum (ML-DSA) passkey. Whether the classical passkey is replaced in place or kept beside it is the method's to say (below). Nobody is asked where the realm offers no ML-DSA algorithm at registration (the default webauthn.algorithms does). Default `pqc-passkey-migration`.

snoozeDays.description: How long Skip puts the activity off for that person. Between 1 and 90. Default 7.

graceDays.description: Counted from the person's FIRST invitation. When it has passed, Skip is gone and the sign-in is held — no session is started — until the activity is done. 0 is no deadline: it can always be skipped. Between 0 and 3650. Default 0.

noPasskey.description: leave: not asked. invite: asked to register a post-quantum passkey, and may always skip it. require: asked, and may skip it only until the allotted time has passed. Default `leave`.

method.description: upgrade: the person uses their classical passkey once, then an ML-DSA passkey replaces it in place on the same authenticator — one passkey, nothing left behind. alongside: an ML-DSA passkey is added beside it, in the post-quantum lane where the realm offers two lanes, or on another authenticator where it offers one. automatic: alongside where the person's passkey policy offers two lanes, upgrade where it offers one. Default `automatic`.

attestation.description: any: its key algorithm is ML-DSA. post-quantum: its key algorithm is ML-DSA AND its recorded attestation was signed with post-quantum algorithms throughout; a passkey with a classical attestation, or none recorded, does not count, and its holder is asked for one that does. Default `any`.

noPasskeyFallback.description: none: ML-DSA only. classical: after an ML-DSA registration fails on the device, a retry with the classical algorithms is offered (where the passkey policy allows one) — a classical passkey is better than a password, and its holder is asked for the migration later like anyone else's. Default `none`.

noPasskeyRole.description: Ignored since #1135: a passkey has no role, so a person with none registers a passkey and nothing else is asked. Accepted so that an older body is not refused; not stored, not answered.

get.summary: What people agreed applications may ask for on their behalf
get.description:
Both halves of the consent register.

**How it works.** With `oauth2.consentRequired` on — it is ON by default, and it is the one policy in this service that is — the authorization endpoint draws `/oauth2/consent` the first time a given username signs in to a given `client_id` for a given scope, and issues nothing until they answer. Allow writes one `oauthConsent` value per scope onto that person's own entry under `ou=users`; Deny returns `access_denied` to the client and records nothing.

**`globals` is CONFIGURATION and `users` is a RECORD**, and the difference decides what removing a row does. A global consent is `oauthGlobalConsent` on an APPLICATION's entry, one value per scope: everybody who signs in to that application skips the prompt for it and nothing is written about anybody — so revoking it asks EVERYBODY again, including the people who would have said yes. A recorded consent is one person's answer, and revoking it asks that one person.

**A delegated permission is recorded by its WHOLE identifier** — `https://example.com/write`, never the bare `write` — because two resources may both expose a permission of that name and a consent to one must not cover the other. `globals[].resource` says which application exposes it where the scope resolves to one, and `globals[].granted` whether that client has also been GRANTED it: the two are independent, and a consented permission the client does not hold is still refused in product mode, and in development when `oauth2.delegatedPermissionsEnforced` is on.

`users[].unreadable` is a value on somebody's entry that is not in the shape this service writes — an `ldapmodify` put it there. It consents nothing and is reported rather than dropped.

`storable: false` means no directory is installed behind the register, so an answer is honoured for one request and forgotten and the screen is drawn every time. That is deliberate: an agreement that cannot be remembered is one nobody gave.

**PAGED, BOTH HALVES, SINCE 2026-09-18.** Each grows without a bound — a recorded consent is one row per (person, application, scope) — so the reply is ONE PAGE of `globals` and one of `users`, each answered by `globalsPaging` and `usersPaging` (`page`, `pages`, `perPage`, `firstRow`, `lastRow`, `total`) and moved by `globalsPage` and `usersPage`; `per` sizes both. `counts` still carries the totals. `q` narrows `users` over the person, the application and the scope, and `matched` is how many it matched. A caller that wants every row walks each half until its `page` equals its `pages`. This is the page `/admin/consent` draws, from the same function.

**`windowed: true` (#820)** means the realm's people are in the store and the recorded half was read a page at a time rather than whole: `usersPaging` is over PEOPLE (`noun: people`) and `matched` and `counts.people` are how many people hold a consent, counted from an index; each page holds every consent of its people, newest first within it; `counts.consents` and `counts.unreadable` are the page's (`counts.countsOf: page`); and `q` is EXACT — a whole username, client_id or scope — with a client_id or scope looked for in at most the first 5,000 holders, `search.complete` saying whether that was everybody. `windowed: false` is the whole register, as described above.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/consent` on the admin console.

200.description: One page of the scopes consented for everybody on an application, one page of the answers people have given, the paging of each, and whether the screen is being drawn at all.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Substring of the person, the application or the scope, case-insensitive. Narrows `users` only. Where the answer is `windowed`, a whole username, client_id or scope instead.

parameters.name: globalsPage
parameters.description: Which page of `globals` to return, answered by `globalsPaging`. The global overrides, configuration on application entries.

parameters.name: usersPage
parameters.description: Which page of `users` to return, answered by `usersPaging`. The recorded consents, one per (person, application, scope), after `q`.

parameters.name: per
parameters.description: Rows per page. Defaults to 50 and is capped at 300. On a drill-down it is SHARED by every list in the reply, which each carry a page number of their own.

post.summary: Consent a scope for everybody who signs in to an application
post.description:
Adds one value to `oauthGlobalConsent` on the application's own entry. Nobody is asked about that scope on that application again, and **nothing is written about anybody** — this is an OVERRIDE and not a record.

That is the whole difference from a person pressing Allow, and it decides what removing it does: `revoke-global-consent` asks everybody again, because there is no record of who would have agreed. Somebody who consented the same scope personally — before or after — still has that on their entry and is still not asked.

**It is keyed on the pair, not on the scope.** Consenting `read` here consents it for THIS application; an application registered five minutes later that spells the same word is still asked. There is no service-wide list of scopes nobody is ever asked about, deliberately: it would mean an application nobody has reviewed inheriting a decision made about a different one.

The scope must be a legal RFC 6749 section 3.3 scope token, because a value with a space in it is two scopes and could never match one. It need NOT name a permission any application defines — most scopes are not permissions, and refusing an unrecognised one would make it impossible to consent `openid`.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/consent` on the admin console.

200.description: The application as it now stands, and what skipping the prompt for that scope now means.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

client.description: The application people sign in to, by its identifier exactly as `ou=applications` holds it. This is the CLIENT — the party that will name the scope in a request — and not the resource that exposes it.

scope.description: The scope, exactly as a client puts it in a `scope` parameter. A delegated permission is its WHOLE identifier.

post.summary: Stop consenting a scope for everybody
post.description:
Removes one value from `oauthGlobalConsent`. **The next person to sign in asking for that scope is PROMPTED**, including everybody the override was covering, because an override records nothing about the people it covers. Somebody who agreed to it personally is unaffected — their answer is on their own entry and `revoke-consent` is what takes that away.

**What was issued under it is revoked (#172).** Every access and refresh token of this application carrying the scope, for everybody but the people who agreed to it themselves, goes on the revocation register every node reads — so it introspects inactive at once — and the instant is written onto the application's entry as `oauthGlobalConsentWithdrawn`, so a refresh token granted before it is refused even if the override is added back. `revoked` is how many tokens this call revoked. **This is the only way to take a global consent away**: the generic `applications/remove` of `oauthGlobalConsent` is refused (`STS-REG-0191`). On one of this service's own surfaces (`sts-admin-console`, `sts-user-portal`, `sts-debugger-ui`) it is not refused either: every session of that surface standing on the override ends at its next token renewal and the person signs in again and is asked.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/consent` on the admin console.

200.description: What was removed, who is asked again, how many tokens were revoked (`revoked`) and when (`withdrawnAt`).

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

post.summary: Take back one answer one person gave
post.description:
Removes the `oauthConsent` value naming this person, this application and this scope. They are asked again the next time that application requests that scope; nobody else is affected.

**All three are required and that is not pedantry.** One person may consent the same scope to several applications, and revoking the wrong pair is invisible until somebody is asked again — which is a week later and looks like a bug in the screen.

A scope covered by GLOBAL consent is not on anybody's entry, so there is nothing here to remove and this refuses rather than pretending: `revoke-global-consent` is the operation for that, and the refusal says so.

**What was issued under it is revoked (#172)**: every access and refresh token this application holds for this person carrying the scope — a refresh token with its whole grant, since withdrawing one scope revokes the whole refresh token — and the instant goes onto their entry as `oauthConsentWithdrawn`, so a refresh token granted before it is refused even after they consent again.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/consent` on the admin console.

200.description: What was removed, what is asked again, how many tokens were revoked (`revoked`) and when (`withdrawnAt`).

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

post.description:
Every `oauthConsent` value naming this person and this application, in one act (#172) — the console's and the API's counterpart of the Withdraw button a person has for each application on `/portal/consents`. They are asked again the next time that application requests anything; every access and refresh token it holds for them under those scopes is revoked; and the instant goes onto their entry, so a refresh token granted before it is refused even after they consent again. Refused when nothing is recorded for the pair — a scope under GLOBAL consent is not on anybody's entry.

post.summary: Forget everything one person agreed to
post.description:
Every `oauthConsent` value on one person's entry, in one call, so that every application asks them again. A separate operation rather than a loop over `revoke-consent` because being asked again is the one thing somebody wants after testing this screen, and doing it a row at a time for a person with thirty consents is a chore rather than a control.

It reaches nothing under GLOBAL consent, because there is nothing on their entry to reach — a scope they were never asked about leaves no record, which is what lets the register tell the two apart at all.

**What was issued under those consents is revoked (#172)**, per application, and each withdrawal instant is written onto their entry — see `revoke-consent`.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/consent` on the admin console.

get.summary: The trust domain: its authorities, its bundle, its listeners
get.description:
What this service is as a SPIFFE issuing authority. The X.509 and JWT authorities (the ACTIVE one first, with the retired ones that are still published behind it), the bundle path and its sequence, every federated trust domain, and whether each of the four gRPC listeners actually bound — which nothing else can tell you, because neither this API nor GET /admin/sts-metadata can see a socket, and `workloadAttestation`: what the Workload API's Unix socket attests, and under `tcp` whether its TCP port is served — in product only where `spiffe.workloadTcpSourceAuthenticated` declares the network authenticates source addresses, on a named address (#166).

The reply also carries `authentication`: whether the SPIRE Server API is enforcing mutual TLS, which identities are administrators, and the whole per-method authorization table, which is SPIRE's own `policy_data.json` row for row.

A Workload API caller on the Unix socket is attested by the workload attestors `spiffe.workloadAttestors` names; one over TCP is identified only by the transport, the endpoint and its address, which is why a product realm refuses a registration entry selecting nothing but the transport and endpoint. An agent's attestation is verified by the attestor its type names or refused (#40, 2026-09-21). Where the SPIRE Server API authenticates nobody, any caller that reaches its port can create a registration entry granting any identity here. GET /spiffe carries the full list of what is and is not checked.

No private key is in this reply. The authority CERTIFICATE is published, as GET /tls/server-certificate publishes that one.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/cert-issuance` on the admin console.

The reply also carries `protocolEndpoints`: every endpoint of this family in the realm the call arrived in, as `{ name, methods, url }` (plus `route` for an HTTP endpoint, `transport` for a socket, and `registered: false` for a route the router no longer has).

200.description: The trust domain, its authorities, its federated bundles and its listeners.

post.summary: Rotate the X.509 authority, the JWT authority, or both
post.description:
ROTATION IS TWO DIFFERENT ACTS. Under the service Root, which is the usual case, it re-issues the SPIFFE Issuing CA and leaves the anchor alone: the X.509 bundle does not change, and SVIDs already in the field go on verifying because their chain still reaches the same Root.

On the self-signed fallback, and for the JWT authority, a new authority is PREPENDED — everything is signed with it from that moment — and the old one stays in the published bundle, whose `spiffe_sequence` changes. Past `spiffe.retainedAuthorities` the oldest is dropped, and anything it signed stops verifying at that moment.

This is also the ONLY way to add an authority to this trust domain. The SPIRE Server API's AppendBundle and PublishJWTAuthority are refused, because they would publish a signing key nothing here holds.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/spiffe` on the admin console.

200.description: What was rotated, and the new bundle sequence.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

post.summary: Add or replace a foreign trust domain's bundle
post.description:
**The bundle is PUSHED here and never PULLED by this service.** The SPIFFE federation specification puts a bundle endpoint URL in the relationship and a real implementation polls it; this one records the URL and refuses to follow it — the SPIRE Server API's RefreshBundle says so in terms — because fetching a URL somebody registered, in order to obtain a key that will then verify credentials, is a server-side request forgery with a citation attached. The same refusal this service gives WS-Federation's `wreqptr` and a client's `jwks_uri`.

**A trust domain this service itself serves is REFUSED** — any realm's, whether or not SPIFFE is on in it (2026-09-12). The bundles are held per realm, and a federated entry naming a served domain would let an authority somebody registered in one realm authenticate workloads as another realm's.

The document is CHECKED, which is unusual for this service: every JWK needs a `use` of `x509-svid`, `jwt-svid` or `wit-svid`, because a consumer MUST IGNORE one without it — so a bundle of keys missing that member is stored happily and then verifies nothing, with no error anywhere pointing back here.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/spiffe` on the admin console.

200.description: Whether it was added or replaced.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

trustDomain.description: The trust domain NAME — `other.example`, not `spiffe://other.example`. This service's own is refused: a trust domain does not federate with itself, and accepting it would give it two bundles that could disagree.

document.description: The bundle, as a JWK Set with `spiffe_sequence` and `spiffe_refresh_hint`. A JSON string is accepted too, which is what the console's textarea sends.

bundleEndpointUrl.description: Recorded and never fetched. It is reported back so an operator can see what the relationship says.

bundleEndpointProfile.description: Which profile the partner expects. Recorded.

endpointSpiffeId.description: For `https_spiffe`, the SPIFFE ID the partner's endpoint presents. Recorded.

get.summary: The registration entries, filtered and paged
get.description:
A registration entry says which SPIFFE ID a workload gets, under which parent, matching which selectors. It is the most important object in a SPIFFE deployment: the Workload API answers out of it.

**The entries ARE the registry.** They live under `ou=entries,ou=spiffe` in the embedded LDAP directory and nothing caches them, so an `ldapmodify` is visible here on the next call and changes what the next SVID looks like.

**The selectors restrict nothing here.** They are recorded, reported, and used by the SPIRE Server API's GetAuthorizedEntries — and the Workload API hands every caller every identity, because nothing in this service attests a workload.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/cert-issuance` on the admin console.

The reply also carries `protocolEndpoints`: every endpoint of this family in the realm the call arrived in, as `{ name, methods, url }` (plus `route` for an HTTP endpoint, `transport` for a socket, and `registered: false` for a route the router no longer has).

200.description: The matching registration entries with the paging that found them, or one entry with its directory entry when `entry` was given.

400.description: The answer.

parameters.name: entry
parameters.description: One entry, by its id — the 32 hex characters this registry minted, which is what the SPIRE Server API calls `id`. The reply then carries that entry with every attribute of its directory entry.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Substring of the SPIFFE ID, the parent, the entry id, the hint or any selector, case-insensitive.

parameters.name: origin
parameters.description: How the entry got here. `auto` is one this service INVENTED for a workload that matched nothing, which is the setting `spiffe.autoCreateEntries` — telling those from entries somebody meant is the whole reason this field exists.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: Which page of the match to return. CLAMPED rather than refused: a page past the end returns the last one, and the reply says which page it actually is.

parameters.name: per
parameters.description: Rows per page. Defaults to 50 and is capped at 300. On a drill-down it is SHARED by every list in the reply, which each carry a page number of their own.

post.summary: Register an identity
post.description:
Three refusals and no others: a SPIFFE ID that is not one, a SPIFFE ID in ANOTHER trust domain (this service is the issuing authority for exactly one, and cannot sign for somebody else's — that is what federation is for), and a SPIFFE ID under the reserved `/spire` path, which belongs to this server and the agents it attests.

A DUPLICATE SPIFFE ID IS ALLOWED. Two entries granting one identity under different parents is a real configuration and SPIRE permits it.

This is the same function `BatchCreateEntry` on the SPIRE Server API calls, writing the same directory entry an `ldapadd` would.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/spiffe/entries` on the admin console.

200.description: The entry as it now stands, with its new id.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

parentId.description: The agent or server it hangs beneath. Defaults to this server's own SPIFFE ID, which is what SPIRE uses for an entry describing a workload rather than a node.

selectors.description: Comma-separated `type:value` pairs, split on the FIRST colon only — so `docker:label:app:web` is type `docker` and value `label:app:web`. An entry with NO selectors matches every workload, which is how a catch-all is written and is also the shape of one somebody forgot to finish.

dnsNames.description: Comma-separated DNS subjectAltNames, added beside the SPIFFE ID. What makes an SVID usable by TLS software that checks a hostname and cannot read a SPIFFE ID.

federatesWith.description: Comma-separated trust domain names whose bundles are handed to a holder of this identity. A name with no bundle here contributes nothing rather than failing.

hint.description: Operator guidance when a workload gets more than one SVID — `internal`, `external`. Passed through verbatim; nothing here reads it.

post.summary: Change one field of an entry
post.description:
**What may be changed is DECLARED and not DERIVED.** The declared half is what the entry may DO — the SPIFFE ID, the parent, the selectors, the DNS names, the lifetimes, the hint, the flags — and it is what the Workload API reads. The derived half is what HAPPENED: the revision number, the SVID counter, when it was created. Those are refused with a list of what is not, because a call that could rewrite them would make this registry lie about the service's own behaviour in a way indistinguishable from the recording being broken.

`ldapmodify` still reaches everything, which is deliberate: refusing it HERE is the difference between offering an operation and merely not preventing it.

The change applies to the NEXT SVID issued from this entry. Nothing already issued changes, and there is nothing to invalidate — SPIFFE has no revocation.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/spiffe/entries` on the admin console.

200.description: The entry as it now stands, at its new revision.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

field.description: Which field. Anything else is refused naming these.

value.description: A list field takes comma-separated values and an empty value CLEARS it; a boolean takes true or false; a TTL takes seconds.

post.summary: Remove an entry
post.description:
Anything holding an SVID minted from it keeps that SVID until it expires. SPIFFE has no revocation — the answer is a short lifetime and rotation, which is why the default X509-SVID lifetime here is an hour and the JWT-SVID one is five minutes.

If this was the LAST entry naming that SPIFFE ID, the identity's directory entry under `ou=users` is marked `spiffeCredentialStatus: revoked` with the reason on it. The entry is NOT deleted, and that flag is not a certificate status: nothing reads it back and no SVID is refused because of it. Deleting one of several entries that name the same identity changes nothing there.

A seeded entry stays deleted until a restart: nothing here is persisted, but nothing re-creates it either, because an operator who deleted it meant to.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/spiffe/entries` on the admin console.

200.description: That it is gone.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

These entries are a RECORD rather than configuration — everything on them was written by this service — which is why nothing about an agent is editable. post.summary: Refuse this agent at AttestAgent
post.description:
ONE OF THE FEW REFUSALS IN THIS SERVICE, and it earns its place: a ban that did not refuse would make the button a lie. A banned agent gets `PermissionDenied` from `AttestAgent`.

Whatever SVID it already holds keeps working until it expires. There is no revocation in SPIFFE, so a ban stops the NEXT identity rather than the current one.

The agent's own entry under `ou=users` — the one every identity this trust domain issues a certificate to gets — is marked `spiffeCredentialStatus: revoked`, and unbanning marks it active again. It is never deleted, and nothing reads that flag back.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/spiffe/agents` on the admin console.

200.description: The agent as it now stands.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

post.description:
How an operator provisions the sidecar agent that serves the Workload API on a Unix socket next to a workload (#324). The SPIRE Server API is what the agent attests to; this is the same join-token store `CreateJoinToken` writes, reached here because there is no admin SVID until a Workload API exists to fetch one from.

The token is shown once, in `token` and in `message`, and is not recorded. `agentSpiffeId` is the identity the token will attest, which is a digest of the token and is safe to keep: parent that agent's workload entries on it. Everything /admin/oidfed draws, out of the same view function: the realm's Entity Identifier and role (trust anchor, intermediate or leaf), its authority hints and federation endpoints, its Federation Entity Keys (public halves, states and history — never a private key), the subordinates it vouches for, the Trust Anchors it trusts, the Trust Mark types it issues, the marks it has issued and carries, the mark policies it publishes as a Trust Anchor, the resolutions it holds, and the claims of its current Entity Configuration — and, for each subordinate, whether it is suspended and its event history, the subordinates it has revoked with theirs (#137), and the Entity Collection crawl it keeps (#136). get.summary: What the authorization server has done in this realm, by mechanism, with the pushed authorization requests still held
get.description:
Everything /admin/oauth2/monitor draws, in SECTIONS — one per mechanism counted, RFC 9126 pushed authorization requests the first. Each section carries its events (the closed vocabulary with a label and a total each), the totals, the OAuth errors returned, one row per client_id with every counter (paged by `clientsPage` and `per`), and — for RFC 9126 — the pushed requests the store still holds, newest first: the digest of the request_uri (its handle; the request_uri itself is not kept), client, authorization server, state, created and expiry, reads, whether and how the client authenticated, form or request object, the redirect_uri and whether section 2.4 let it in unregistered, the DPoP key, and the parameters. That list is paged by `offset` and `limit` (or the console's `page` and `per`) and filtered by `state` and `client_id`. RFC 9470's step-up is the second section (`stepup`), its clients paged by `stepUpClientsPage`, carrying the requirement this service's own resource server enforces (`ownResourceRequirement`) and `acrValuesSupported`. Per trust realm, merged across processes, and with no reset.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/oauth2/monitor` on the admin console.

200.description: The sections, their counters and the pushed requests held.

post.summary: Withdraw a pushed authorization request (RFC 9126)
post.description:
Removes one pushed request, named by the SHA-256 of its request_uri, from this realm's store of pushed authorization requests, live or spent. The authorization endpoint refuses it from then on with 400 invalid_request_uri, exactly as it refuses one that expired and was swept; a browser already on the sign-in or consent screen with it is refused when it comes back. Counted as `par.deleted` and written to the audit log. A value that is not a handle (43 characters of base64url), or one this realm does not hold, is refused 400. The store keeps no request_uri (#614), so the handle is the only name it answers to.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/oauth2/monitor` on the admin console.

200.description: The handle withdrawn, the client it was bound to and the state it was in.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

post.summary: Start a post-login activity
post.description:
Starts a post-login activity in this realm. AT SIGN-IN, from now, each person it reaches is asked to do it (#1126), under the rules of the post-login profile that reaches them — even where that profile is off, unless it is a NAMED profile that is off, which excludes them. BY MAIL, from the next run of the scheduler job `post-login.activity-mail` (every few minutes, or Run now on Monitoring → Scheduler) each person the activity is DUE for — it reaches them, the realm can make the passkey, they have not done it — is mailed at the address on their entry a reminder to sign in, at most `maxMails` times and never twice inside `intervalDays`. The mail's one link opens the sign-in page; it carries no credential, and the post-login activity does the registration. `groups` narrows the people to the members of those groups: their UNION, a person in two of them read and mailed once; none means everybody in the realm. A group this realm does not have is refused (STS-AUTHN-0530); a second started activity for the same activity and the same groups is refused (STS-AUTHN-0492); bad values are STS-AUTHN-0490.

**Mirrors** `POST /admin/post-login-activities` on the admin console.

400.description: The operation was refused; `errors` says why and nothing changed.

get.summary: The federation partners whose Shared Signals this realm receives
get.description:
Everything /admin/ssf/transmitters draws: each federation relationship whose signals are on (its kind — `sign-in` or `signals-only` — SSF issuer, discovered configuration, delivery, stream, counts and blocks), every Security Event Token that arrived with whether it verified, the person it named and what it led to, the sign-ins partners have blocked and the account locks a signals-only partner put on people here. Never a secret. `relationship` narrows what arrived. What arrived, the blocks and the locks are each one page, moved by `receivedPage`, `blocksPage` and `locksPage` with `per` shared, and described by `paging`. A partner's stream is configured on its relationship and acted on with `POST /admin-api/federation/signals-*`.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/ssf/transmitters` on the admin console.

200.description: The report.

parameters.name: relationship
parameters.description: Only what arrived from this relationship. Applied before what arrived is paged.

parameters.name: receivedPage
parameters.description: Which page of what arrived, newest first. Clamped, like every page parameter here.

parameters.name: blocksPage
parameters.description: Which page of the sign-ins partners blocked.

parameters.name: locksPage
parameters.description: Which page of the account locks partners put on people here.

parameters.name: per
parameters.description: Rows per page, shared by the three lists.

get.summary: Check the held audit rows against their checksums
get.description: Each row carries a keyed checksum whose key is not in the database, and the checksum of the row its process wrote before it. `altered` lists the seq of any row that no longer matches. `missing` lists each place a row is gone from between two held rows of one process. `head` says whether this process's newest row is still there: `intact`; `truncated` when its newest rows were removed; `altered` when the record of which row is newest was changed; `none` when it has written no signed row. The oldest rows leave by design at `audit.maxEvents`. `unsigned` counts rows written with no key-encryption key in the process.

200.description: The result.
